title: Quantum-Classical Hybrid Methods for Optimization: Lessons from Classical Decomposition

paper.title: Quantum-Classical Hybrid Methods for Optimization: Lessons from Classical Decomposition
paper.abstract:
Abstract Quantum and physics-inspired solvers provide specialized sampling interfaces for Ising and quadratic unconstrained binary optimization models, but constrained optimization requires broader coordination and certification.
This survey uses classical decomposition to analyze how such solvers can be integrated into hybrid quantum-classical algorithms.
We distinguish formal decomposition, reformulation and reduction, and computational orchestration.
For each interface, we ask what the transformation preserves, which assumptions make the outer method converge, and which certificates the implemented inner routine supplies.
The central questions are whether that information meets the classical algorithm’s requirements and whether hybridization improves solution quality or total cost enough to justify its coordination overhead.
Benders decomposition, column generation, graph reduction, and copositive methods illustrate this distinction by separating heuristic proposals from classical certification.
We also distinguish component effects within a fixed wrapper, reduction–solver interactions, and comparisons between complete quantum-enabled and classical systems.
The analyzed studies provide conditional component benefits and favorable co-design evidence, but do not establish transferable end-to-end superiority over strong classical comparators.
The resulting framework identifies opportunities for constraint programming and operations research in structure-preserving design, safeguarded hybrid algorithms, and controlled benchmarking. Keywords: quantum optimization; hybrid quantum-classical algorithms; decomposition; constraint programming; certification; benchmarking.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Classical optimization makes discrete problems tractable by exploiting structure, coordinating tasks that are easier for suitable solvers, and combining their results. Quantum optimization adds specialized solvers that encode an objective in a physical system or a sequence of controlled quantum operations, then return sampled candidate assignments. Section 3.3 introduces these quantum terms for readers without a quantum information science background. Using them for general constrained models requires additional encoding, classical coordination, or both. Decomposition connects specialized solvers to broader algorithms through interfaces such as pricing, recourse evaluation, and separation. The output required at an interface may be a useful candidate, a valid inequality, or a certified bound. We ask which outputs a quantum routine can supply, which classical checks remain necessary, and whether the resulting hybrid improves quality or total computational cost, including coordination overhead, over suitable classical alternatives. Existing reviews describe Ising machines ( Mohseni et al., 2022 ) , the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) and its variants ( Blekos et al., 2024 ) , the wider opportunities and obstacles in quantum optimization ( Abbas et al., 2024 ) , and, in a recent preprint, learned control of adaptive quantum workflows ( Lau, 2026 ) . Our contribution is to analyze these topics jointly through interface requirements, guarantees, and performance attribution . Tables 2 and 3 apply this analysis to the surveyed algorithm families, distinguishing returned candidates from the certificates required for guarantees. Section 5 then assesses the reported studies through component comparisons, reduction–solver interactions, and complete-system comparisons. The resulting conclusions concern the purposive corpus described in Appendix A , with eligibility through October 12, 2026. Section 2 introduces the classical foundations; Section 3 maps mixed-integer models to Ising and QUBO form and introduces the quantum algorithms and hardware that accept them. Section 4 develops the hybrid architectures, Section 5 evaluates their evidence, and Section 6 identifies design questions for constraint programming and operations research.

sections.heading: 2.1 What can be expressed, and why it is hard
sections.text: Mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) is a very expressive modeling language. A general MINLP has the form minimize x , y \displaystyle\underset{x,y}{\operatorname{minimize}} f ⁡ ( x , y ) \displaystyle f(x,y) (1) subject ​ to \displaystyle\operatorname{subject\ to} g ⁡ ( x , y ) ≤ 0 , \displaystyle g(x,y)\leq 0, x ∈ ℝ n c , y ∈ ℤ n i , \displaystyle x\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{c}},\quad y\in\mathbb{Z}^{n_{i}}, with f f and g g possibly nonlinear and nonconvex. The n c n_{c} continuous variables represent quantities, the n i n_{i} integer variables represent choices, and nonlinear terms may represent physical relationships. Applications include process design, scheduling, and engineering optimization ( Biegler and Grossmann, 2004 ) . The convex-MINLP solver review ( Kronqvist et al., 2019 ) and the fifty-year perspective on MINLP and disjunctive programming ( Kronqvist et al., 2026 ) trace the algorithms and formulations behind this modeling capability. Even linear integer programming is NP-hard; practical methods exploit instance structure, whereas quantum Ising/quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) interfaces require additional encodings to represent the constrained form above. This survey focuses on a single objective. Quantum multiobjective methods can instead explore trade-offs by approximately solving or sampling scalarized problems with different objective weights ( Kotil et al., 2025 ) . Many interface and certification considerations below apply to those subproblems, although solving individual scalarizations does not by itself certify a complete Pareto front.

sections.heading: 2.2 Decomposition as the engine of progress
sections.text: Master problem complicating (integer) variables y y Subproblem remaining variables x x , with y y held fixed trial values y ^ \hat{y} optimality / feasibility cuts Figure 1: Classical Benders coordination: the master proposes complicating variables y y ; classical recourse in x x returns valid cuts. Hybrid interfaces are compared in Section 4 . Classical solver studies report large aggregate gains from algorithms and hardware ( Bixby, 2012 ; Koch et al., 2022 ) ; they do not isolate decomposition’s causal share. Decomposition is one important way to exploit problem structure. The idea: split a problem into smaller or more tractable parts, then coordinate them. In Benders decomposition, fixing complicating variables leaves a linear subproblem whose dual generates cuts for a master problem ( Benders, 1962 ) . Generalized Benders extends this construction to nonlinear subproblems through convex duality, making it relevant to MINLP ( Geoffrion, 1972 ) . Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition reformulates a structured linear program over the extreme points and, when necessary, extreme rays of its blocks, pricing columns as needed ( Dantzig and Wolfe, 1960 ) ; this underlies column generation and branch-and-price ( Barnhart et al., 1998 ; Lübbecke and Desrosiers, 2005 ) . For convex MINLP under standard subproblem and regularity assumptions, outer approximation alternates between a mixed-integer linear master and continuous nonlinear subproblems, accumulating valid supporting linearizations until the bounds meet ( Duran and Grossmann, 1986 ) . For nonconvex MINLP, local linearizations need not give valid global bounds; deterministic global methods combine valid relaxations with domain partitioning and bound tightening to certify a solution ( Burer and Letchford, 2012 ) . In Figure 1 , the outgoing assignment fixes the complicating variables y y ; the return cuts exclude infeasible master choices or bound their recourse cost. These cuts improve the master’s relaxation, whereas a candidate assignment alone supplies no such bound. Other decompositions use different master variables and oracle interfaces, as summarized in Section 4 . Logic-based Benders provides a bridge to constraint programming: cuts follow from an inference dual, allowing subproblems whose proofs need not come from linear programming duality ( Hooker and Ottosson, 2003 ) . Surveys and textbooks develop the theory and implementation of these methods ( Rahmaniani et al., 2017 ; Conejo et al., 2006 ; Constante-Flores and Conejo, 2025 ; Conforti et al., 2014 ) . Their interfaces require more than candidate assignments: cut validity, bounds, and termination each have proof obligations. We adapt a classical decomposition taxonomy ( Constante-Flores and Conejo, 2025 ) into three composable structural descriptions: • Formal decomposition splits variables, constraints, or the search domain. Its duality-based forms include Benders ( Benders, 1962 ) , Dantzig–Wolfe ( Dantzig and Wolfe, 1960 ) , and augmented Lagrangian methods such as the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) ( Boyd et al., 2011 ) ; its recursive forms include branching with bound-based pruning, as in branch and bound ( Land and Doig, 1960 ) . • Reformulation and reduction transform the problem through penalty mappings, conic lifts, coarsening, or elimination. An exact reformulation preserves the relevant solutions and objective; an approximation may change them. A relaxation supplies a lower bound in minimization (upper in maximization) by enlarging the feasible region or underestimating (overestimating) the objective. • Orchestration coordinates routines through samples, parameters, or candidate solutions. For example, an outer optimizer can tune the parameters of a quantum routine using the objective values estimated from its outputs; this parameter-tuning loop can itself be nested inside a decomposition. Section 4 uses these categories to distinguish formal master–subproblem methods, graph and conic reformulations, and sampling or parameter-tuning orchestration. They identify algorithmic structure, not mutually exclusive guarantee classes. An exact conic reformulation can support cutting-plane methods ( Brown et al., 2024 ) or Frank–Wolfe updates ( Frank and Wolfe, 1956 ; Yurtsever et al., 2022 ) , but heuristic inner solves require separate convergence justification. Conversely, a formal decomposition may lack its classical guarantee when convexity, oracle accuracy, or certified pruning assumptions fail. We therefore assess three questions independently: what the transformation preserves, which assumptions make the outer method converge, and which certificates the implemented inner routine supplies. The practical lesson is to assign each solver a task that exploits structure and whose output can be verified. Smaller subproblems can help, but duplicated work, many iterations, or lost global structure can erase that benefit. Dimension reduction alone establishes neither computational savings nor a potential quantum contribution.

sections.heading: 3 Quantum and physics-inspired solvers for Ising and QUBO problems
sections.text: This section first states the classical models that Ising and quantum solvers accept and how mixed-integer problems can be translated into them (Sections 3.1 and 3.2 ). It then introduces the quantum concepts used in the rest of the article (Section 3.3 ), the main quantum optimization algorithms (Section 3.4 ), and the hardware and physics-inspired platforms that run them (Section 3.5 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 The Ising and QUBO substrate
sections.text: Here the Ising objective is the energy of a finite, classical, pairwise spin model on a graph G = ( V , ℰ ) G=(V,\mathcal{E}) , with vertices V V and edges ℰ \mathcal{E} : E ⁡ ( s ) = ∑ i ∈ V h i ​ s i + ∑ { i , j } ∈ ℰ J i ​ j ​ s i ​ s j , s i ∈ { − 1 , 1 } . E(s)=\sum_{i\in V}h_{i}s_{i}+\sum_{\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{E}}J_{ij}s_{i}s_{j},\qquad s_{i}\in\{-1,1\}. (2) The real coefficients h i h_{i} are external fields, or single-spin biases, and J i ​ j J_{ij} are pairwise couplings; their signs are included in the coefficients. Fixing spins in a set V fix ⊆ V V_{\mathrm{fix}}\subseteq V leaves each remaining spin i i with the effective local field h i + ∑ j ∈ V fix : { i , j } ∈ ℰ J i ​ j s j h_{i}+\sum_{j\in V_{\mathrm{fix}}:\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{E}}J_{ij}s_{j} , its new linear coefficient. Under the displayed plus-sign convention, J i ​ j < 0 J_{ij}<0 favors aligned spins (a ferromagnetic coupling), whereas J i ​ j > 0 J_{ij}>0 favors opposite spins (an antiferromagnetic coupling). The graph and coefficients are problem data, with no restriction to a regular interaction graph or couplings of one sign. This specifies the optimization model within the broader physics tradition of Ising ferromagnets and disordered spin glasses ( Ising, 1925 ; Sherrington and Kirkpatrick, 1975 ) . Finding a ground-state configuration means minimizing E ⁡ ( s ) E(s) . The affine substitution s i = 2 ​ x i − 1 s_{i}=2x_{i}-1 , with inverse x i = ( s i + 1 ) / 2 x_{i}=(s_{i}+1)/2 , maps spin assignments bijectively to bits and converts the energy into an equivalent quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem min x ∈ { 0 , 1 } n x ⊤ ​ Q ​ x , \min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\quad x^{\top}Qx, (3) where n = | V | n=|V| and Q ∈ ℝ n × n Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is symmetric. Off-diagonal entries are half the coefficients of the equivalent upper-triangular convention because x ⊤ ​ Q ​ x x^{\top}Qx counts each pair twice. Linear terms occupy the diagonal, since x i 2 = x i x_{i}^{2}=x_{i} ; additive constants do not change the minimizer and are dropped. Conversely, substituting x i = ( s i + 1 ) / 2 x_{i}=(s_{i}+1)/2 into x ⊤ ​ Q ​ x x^{\top}Qx gives ( 2 ), up to a constant, with J i ​ j = Q i ​ j / 2 J_{ij}=Q_{ij}/2 for i < j i<j and h i = 1 2 ​ ∑ j Q i ​ j h_{i}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}Q_{ij} . The maximum-cut problem partitions vertices into two sets to maximize the weight of crossing edges. With nonnegative edge weights w i ​ j w_{ij} , it maximizes ∑ { i , j } ∈ ℰ w i ​ j ​ ( 1 − s i ​ s j ) / 2 \sum_{\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{E}}w_{ij}(1-s_{i}s_{j})/2 , since an edge contributes exactly when its spins differ ( Goemans and Williamson, 1995 ) . Negation gives, up to a constant, a zero-field Ising minimization with J i ​ j = w i ​ j / 2 J_{ij}=w_{ij}/2 ; the affine substitution above produces a QUBO. A physical solver returns samples from a device- and protocol-dependent distribution, typically without an optimality certificate. Ising-oriented devices include quantum annealers, optical and analog machines, and digital accelerators, with applications in optimization and engineering ( Mohseni et al., 2022 ; Bernal et al., 2022 ) ; Section 3.5 describes these platforms.

A ​ x ≤ b Ax\leq b x ∈ { 0 , 1 } n x\in\{0,1\}^{n} Penalized form min ⁡ f ⁡ ( x ) \min\;f(x) + ρ ​ ∥ A ​ x + S ​ w − b ∥ 2 +\,\rho\,\lVert Ax+Sw-b\rVert^{2} slack bits w w , u = S ​ w u=Sw QUBO min ⁡ ( x , w ) ⊤ ​ Q ​ ( x , w ) \min\;(x,w)^{\top}Q\,(x,w) additional bits, coefficient range constraints into objective absorb slacks, tune ρ \rho Figure 2: Constraint-to-QUBO mapping for integer or scaled-rational data and a quadratic objective (after any required quadratization). Exact slack encoding u = S ​ w u=Sw , with binary slack bits w w and encoding matrix S S , requires bounded ranges commensurate with the encoding; arbitrary real coefficients need not admit it. Here Q Q acts on the concatenated bits ( x , w ) (x,w) . Slack bits are auxiliaries; squaring the penalty introduces pairwise couplings, and weights satisfying ( 4 ) preserve optima. The larger model and coefficient range can worsen conditioning and increase the selected solver’s resource requirements. The MINLP ( 1 ) is the natural starting point for these mappings: the task is to represent general integer, continuous, and nonlinear structure, not only to penalize constraints. Standard catalogs and modeling tutorials describe the resulting formulations ( Lucas, 2014 ; Glover et al., 2019 ) . Reaching ( 3 ) involves four steps, each with its own cost. Below, x x denotes the encoded binary vector. First, each integer variable is written in binary: for z ∈ { L , … , U } z\in\{L,\ldots,U\} , a binary encoding is z = L + ∑ k = 0 m − 1 2 k ​ b k z=L+\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}2^{k}b_{k} , with m = ⌈ log 2 ⁡ ( U − L + 1 ) ⌉ m=\lceil\log_{2}(U-L+1)\rceil and b k ∈ { 0 , 1 } b_{k}\in\{0,1\} . If the bit range exceeds U − L U-L , the constraint ∑ k 2 k ​ b k ≤ U − L \sum_{k}2^{k}b_{k}\leq U-L or a bounded encoding must exclude excess values. Second, continuous variables must either be discretized, which introduces an additional approximation, or remain with a classical solver; the latter is the decomposition route of Section 4 . Third, nonlinear terms must become quadratic. Once the variables are binary, every real-valued function of them has an exact multilinear polynomial representation, for example e b = 1 + ( e − 1 ) ​ b e^{b}=1+(e-1)\,b for b ∈ { 0 , 1 } b\in\{0,1\} , although the representation can need exponentially many terms; auxiliary variables that represent products, enforced by penalty terms, then reduce it to quadratic form ( Boros and Hammer, 2002 ) . Approximating a function to keep the model small is a separate modeling choice, distinct from the approximation introduced by discretizing continuous variables. Fourth, constraints can become objective penalties, but there is no universal encoding. A linear equality can use ρ ​ ( a ⊤ ​ x − b ) 2 \rho(a^{\top}x-b)^{2} ; an inequality can first introduce a nonnegative slack, whose exact positional binary encoding requires bounded, commensurate values, as in integer or scaled-rational data. Reading Figure 2 from left to right reveals two resource costs: slack bits enlarge the assignment, and squaring a constraint introduces pairwise couplings between its variables. A compact constrained model can therefore become a denser QUBO with a wider coefficient range. Direct penalties can avoid slack bits when the constraint has suitable structure: for binary variables, ρ ​ x i ​ x j \rho x_{i}x_{j} penalizes exactly the violation of x i + x j ≤ 1 x_{i}+x_{j}\leq 1 . One-hot encodings assign one bit to each allowed integer value and require exactly one selected bit; they use more bits than positional encodings but can simplify selection constraints. Higher-order violation penalties may instead require quadratization auxiliaries ( Lucas, 2014 ; Glover et al., 2019 ; Quintero et al., 2022 ) . Eliminating variables, preserving feasibility in the quantum algorithm (Section 3.4 ), or retaining constraints in a classical master (Section 4 ) offers alternatives to a single penalized QUBO. These choices trade variable count, coupling density, coefficient range, and proof requirements; large penalty weights stretch the range a physical solver must resolve, and samples can remain infeasible. Penalization changes the feasible domain, even when it preserves global optima ( Constante-Flores and Conejo, 2025 ) . Let 𝒳 ⊆ { 0 , 1 } n \mathcal{X}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n} be the finite encoded domain, let F ⊆ 𝒳 F\subseteq\mathcal{X} be the nonempty feasible set, let P ⁡ ( x ) ≥ 0 P(x)\geq 0 be a penalty function vanishing exactly on F F , and let f ⋆ = min x ∈ F ⁡ f ⁡ ( x ) f^{\star}=\min_{x\in F}f(x) . Then, for 𝒳 ∖ F ≠ ∅ \mathcal{X}\setminus F\neq\varnothing , the penalized problem min x ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ f ⁡ ( x ) + ρ ​ P ​ ( x ) \min_{x\in\mathcal{X}}f(x)+\rho\,P(x) has the same global minimizers and optimal value as the constrained problem whenever ρ > max ⁡ { 0 , max x ∈ 𝒳 ∖ F ⁡ f ⋆ − f ⁡ ( x ) P ⁡ ( x ) } . \rho>\max\left\{0,\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}\setminus F}\frac{f^{\star}-f(x)}{P(x)}\right\}. (4) The threshold is finite but involves the unknown f ⋆ f^{\star} ; an arbitrary penalty weight need not preserve the optimum. If 𝒳 = F \mathcal{X}=F , any ρ ≥ 0 \rho\geq 0 suffices. One sufficient, possibly conservative bound is ρ > ( f ¯ − f ¯ ) / δ \rho>(\overline{f}-\underline{f})/\delta , where f ¯ ≤ f ⁡ ( x ) \underline{f}\leq f(x) on 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , f ¯ \overline{f} is the value of a known feasible solution, and every infeasible point has penalty at least δ > 0 \delta>0 . Problem-specific formulations can give sharper weights and smaller encodings; catalogs discuss many examples ( Lucas, 2014 ; Glover et al., 2019 ) , and the maximum k k -colorable subgraph analysis explicitly characterizes penalty choices and auxiliary-variable trade-offs ( Quintero et al., 2022 ) . The broader theory of Lagrangian reformulation distinguishes equality of optimal values from equality of minimizer sets and gives sufficient conditions for finite exact penalties ( Quintero et al., 2024 ) . In particular, a positive minimum penalty over infeasible points is automatic on the finite domain used in ( 4 ), whereas continuous domains can require limiting penalty sequences rather than a finite exact weight. Maximum independent set (MIS) illustrates the mapping. Given a graph G = ( V , ℰ ) G=(V,\mathcal{E}) , MIS asks for as many vertices as possible with no edge between two selected vertices; as a mixed-integer program (MIP), max ⁡ ∑ v ∈ V x ∈ { 0 , 1 } V ⁡ x v s.t. x u + x v ≤ 1 for all ​ { u , v } ∈ ℰ . \max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{V}}\ \sum_{v\in V}x_{v}\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad x_{u}+x_{v}\leq 1\quad\text{for all }\{u,v\}\in\mathcal{E}. Penalizing each edge with both endpoints selected gives the QUBO min x ∈ { 0 , 1 } V − ∑ v ∈ V x v + ρ ​ ∑ { u , v } ∈ ℰ x u ​ x v . \min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{V}}\ -\sum_{v\in V}x_{v}+\rho\sum_{\{u,v\}\in\mathcal{E}}x_{u}x_{v}. Any ρ > 1 \rho>1 satisfies ( 4 ), because deleting one endpoint of each such edge yields an independent set that is smaller by at most the number of penalized edges. Arrays of individually controlled neutral atoms can instead realize MIS natively on unit-disk graphs; the interaction mechanism and its restrictions are explained in Section 3.5 . Modeling software automates parts of this translation and differs in what it delivers. QUBO.jl supports mathematical-programming reformulations and solver access ( Xavier et al., 2026 ) ; Qiskit Optimization converts quadratic programs into QUBO form when they have no continuous variables, no quadratic constraints, and integer-valued coefficients in all linear constraints ( Qiskit Community, n.d. ) ; and D-Wave’s open-source dimod library represents binary and constrained quadratic models, converting a constrained model into a penalized binary model only when its constraints are linear and its integer variables have zero lower bounds ( D-Wave Quantum, n.d.a ) . PyQUBO supports symbolic QUBO construction and constraint-aware decoding ( Zaman et al., 2022 ) , and qubovert manages polynomial and constrained Boolean or spin formulations ( Iosue, n.d. ) . Fixstars Amplify SDK combines modeling and conversion with access to several quantum and classical solver backends ( Fixstars Amplify, n.d. ) . Such libraries build and transform models locally, whereas hosted solver services, discussed in Section 4.4 , also execute them. The interface automates parts of the translation; its choice alone establishes neither exactness of a penalty model nor a quantum contribution.

sections.heading: 3.3 Quantum computation for optimization readers
sections.text: A classical bit takes value 0 or 1; a qubit is a quantum system with two distinguished states, written | 0 ⟩ |0\rangle and | 1 ⟩ |1\rangle . For n n qubits, the computational basis consists of 2 n 2^{n} mutually orthogonal vectors | x ⟩ |x\rangle , one for each binary assignment x x ; the ket notation | ⋅ ⟩ |\cdot\rangle denotes a state vector ( Nielsen and Chuang, 2010 ) . An ideal pure state is a normalized superposition | ψ ⟩ = ∑ x α x ​ | x ⟩ |\psi\rangle=\sum_{x}\alpha_{x}|x\rangle , where the complex amplitudes satisfy ∑ x | α x | 2 = 1 \sum_{x}|\alpha_{x}|^{2}=1 . Measuring in this basis returns one assignment x x with probability | α x | 2 |\alpha_{x}|^{2} , not all assignments at once. Repeated preparation and measurement produce samples. Unlike classical probabilities, amplitudes have phases: when combined, they can reinforce or cancel, producing interference that changes the sampling probabilities. A product state factors into individual-qubit states; a pure state that does not is entangled . A Hamiltonian H H is a Hermitian matrix (equal to its conjugate transpose) representing energy, with real eigenvalues. For a classical cost f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) , the diagonal problem Hamiltonian satisfies H C ​ | x ⟩ = f ⁡ ( x ) ​ | x ⟩ H_{C}|x\rangle=f(x)|x\rangle ; its lowest-energy, or ground, states encode minimizing assignments. Quantum evolution is the change of the amplitudes over time. For constant H H , ideal closed-system evolution applies U ⁡ ( t ) = e − i ​ t ​ H U(t)=e^{-\mathrm{i}tH} , where i 2 = − 1 \mathrm{i}^{2}=-1 , setting the reduced Planck constant ℏ = 1 \hbar=1 ; this linear map is unitary, meaning reversible and norm-preserving. Optimization algorithms choose these operations to make good assignments more likely upon measurement; doing so efficiently is the algorithmic challenge. Analog devices physically implement a Hamiltonian and vary its coefficients continuously. Figure 3 illustrates how energy levels change along such a path; Section 3.4 explains the annealing method. Gate-model computers compose quantum gates , unitary operations on one or a few qubits, into a circuit , followed here by measurement. A designed Hamiltonian evolution is implemented or approximated by such a gate sequence. The upper part of Figure 4 illustrates this circuit notation: each horizontal wire carries one qubit through operations ordered from left to right, and the final measurements produce the bits of one assignment. The gates marked 𝖧 \mathsf{H} prepare ( | 0 ⟩ + | 1 ⟩ ) / 2 (|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2} from each | 0 ⟩ |0\rangle ; these Hadamard gates are distinct from the Hamiltonian H H . Circuit width counts qubits; gate depth counts sequential layers of operations that cannot run in parallel. Gate platforms include superconducting circuits, trapped ions, photonics ( Bharti et al., 2022 ) , and neutral atoms ( Henriet et al., 2020 ) . Noise and control error perturb the ideal operations; fault-tolerant computation uses many physical qubits to encode logical qubits and correct errors, at substantial resource cost. Progress from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) regime, whose gates lack error-correction protection ( Preskill, 2018 ) toward early fault tolerance now includes demonstrations of error correction and logical operations, while large-scale fault-tolerant systems remain a development goal ( Bluvstein et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Adiabatic computation and quantum annealing.
sections.text: Adiabatic quantum computation starts from an easily prepared ground state and slowly changes the Hamiltonian, aiming to follow its evolving ground state ( Albash and Lidar, 2018 ) . Quantum annealing commonly uses H ⁡ ( t ) = A ⁡ ( t ) ​ H D + B ⁡ ( t ) ​ H C H(t)=A(t)H_{D}+B(t)H_{C} , decreasing the driver weight A ⁡ ( t ) A(t) while increasing the problem weight B ⁡ ( t ) B(t) ( Kadowaki and Nishimori, 1998 ) . The usual driver H D = − ∑ i X i H_{D}=-\sum_{i}X_{i} is a transverse field : X i X_{i} exchanges | 0 ⟩ |0\rangle and | 1 ⟩ |1\rangle on qubit i i , so this term couples assignments differing in one bit. Its ground state is the uniform superposition of assignments, also prepared by the Hadamard gates in the circuit example of Figure 4 . “Transverse” refers to its orientation perpendicular to the spin axis used for the diagonal Ising objective; its evolution redistributes amplitudes between assignments. Figure 3 plots the two lowest instantaneous energies against progress τ = t / T ann ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \tau=t/T_{\mathrm{ann}}\in[0,1] , where T ann T_{\mathrm{ann}} is the annealing duration. For the nondegenerate levels shown, their vertical separation Δ spec ​ ( τ ) = E 1 ​ ( τ ) − E 0 ​ ( τ ) \Delta_{\mathrm{spec}}(\tau)=E_{1}(\tau)-E_{0}(\tau) is the spectral gap; it concerns the evolving Hamiltonian, rather than an incumbent’s objective gap to optimality. The adiabatic strategy is to remain in the lower level as its associated state changes. Near the marked minimum gap, transitions out of that state can be difficult to suppress; a slower schedule may be required, with the sufficient runtime also depending on how the Hamiltonian changes and the allowed error ( Albash and Lidar, 2018 ) . Thus the minimum gap alone neither specifies a runtime nor establishes a computational advantage. Finite temperature, control error, and restricted connectivity further limit the transfer of closed-system guarantees to implemented annealers ( Hauke et al., 2020 ) . Implemented annealing is therefore assessed as a sampling heuristic, with analog evolution realized continuously in hardware. annealing progress τ = t / T ann \tau=t/T_{\mathrm{ann}} energy (schematic) Δ spec , min \Delta_{\mathrm{spec},\min} E 0 ​ ( τ ) E_{0}(\tau) E 1 ​ ( τ ) E_{1}(\tau) 0 0 1 1 Figure 3: Illustrative instantaneous energy levels along an annealing path. Only the ground level E 0 E_{0} (solid) and first excited level E 1 E_{1} (dashed) are shown; their closest approach marks the minimum spectral gap Δ spec , min \Delta_{\mathrm{spec},\min} . These curves depict a schematic spectrum, not measured device performance. TikZ code prepared with OpenAI Codex assistance.

sections.heading: Variational algorithms.
sections.text: In the circuit-based variational algorithms considered here, a classical optimizer adjusts parameters of a gate-based circuit. For each parameter choice, repeated executions estimate a training objective, often the expected problem cost ( Cerezo et al., 2021 ; Bharti et al., 2022 ) . An ansatz is the chosen family of states generated by the parameterized circuit; choosing it fixes the search space. The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) estimates the expected energy of a parameterized state and uses a classical optimizer to lower it, seeking the Hamiltonian’s smallest eigenvalue and an associated state ( Peruzzo et al., 2014 ) . For a cost Hamiltonian diagonal in the computational basis, this energy is estimated by the mean objective value of the sampled assignments. The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) typically starts from an equal-amplitude superposition of all assignments and applies p p layers, each a problem evolution followed by a mixing evolution ( Farhi et al., 2014b ; Zhou et al., 2020 ) . At layer ℓ \ell , the problem step e − i ​ γ ℓ ​ H C e^{-\mathrm{i}\gamma_{\ell}H_{C}} changes each assignment’s phase according to its cost; alone, it leaves sampling probabilities unchanged and is not a descent step. The mixing step e − i ​ β ℓ ​ H M e^{-\mathrm{i}\beta_{\ell}H_{M}} , commonly with H M = ∑ i X i H_{M}=\sum_{i}X_{i} , transfers amplitude between assignments, allowing interference to change their probabilities. In Figure 4 , the dashed enclosure repeats this pair p p times without intermediate measurement; each wide block must be compiled into gates, so p p is not the physical gate depth. For fixed angles ( β ℓ , γ ℓ ) ℓ = 1 p (\beta_{\ell},\gamma_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{p} , fresh executions yield assignments whose costs define the training objective; the return arrow carries these samples to the classical optimizer, which selects the next set of 2 ​ p 2p angles. This outer loop seeks angles that improve the training objective without guaranteeing descent or optimality; it is distinct from the mixer’s transitions within one circuit (Section 4.1 ). Warm-start QAOA maps a classical relaxation solution to initial qubit amplitudes and adapts the mixer ( Egger et al., 2021 ) . sections.heading: Constraints inside quantum algorithms.
sections.text: Constraints that are not penalized can enter the quantum algorithm itself. The feasibility-preserving generalization of QAOA starts with amplitudes only on feasible assignments and uses mixers whose ideal transitions stay within that set ( Hadfield et al., 2019 ) ; implementation errors can violate this invariance. Linear Ising penalties use single-spin biases rather than extra pairwise couplings and can reduce connectivity and coefficient-range demands, with theoretical, simulation, and annealing-hardware evidence for the studied constraints ( Mirkarimi et al., 2024b ; Mirkarimi et al., 2024a ) . Embedding Lagrangian duality in adiabatic computation can avoid slack-variable encodings; in a fault-tolerant circuit implementation, the proposed construction has a qubit count independent of the number of constraints, while solution-sampling probabilities still depend on the duality gap and complementary slackness ( Gabbassov et al., 2025 ) . Variational methods can also keep multipliers or slack variables classical. A transaction-settlement method updates circuit parameters and nonnegative slack variables, with sample-informed slack adjustments intended to escape poor local solutions ( Braine et al., 2021 ) . A variational quantum eigensolver with constraints (VQEC) uses quantum estimates of costs, constraints, and gradients while a classical primal–dual method updates circuit parameters and Lagrange multipliers ( Le and Kekatos, 2024 ) . Its expectation-constrained formulations can admit distributions containing infeasible assignments, and its nonconvex parameter updates have no general global-convergence guarantee; individual samples still require the original feasibility checks. Quantum Zeno constraint enforcement instead repeatedly measures whether the state lies in the subspace spanned by feasible assignments, without identifying the full assignment. Frequent checks suppress transitions out of that subspace in the ideal limit; finite measurement rates and implementation errors must be assessed in practice ( Herman et al., 2023 ; Berwald et al., 2025 ) . Thus constraints can enter through objective penalties, dual multipliers, or restrictions on the quantum evolution. Linear penalty constructions need not satisfy the assumptions of ( 4 ); their feasibility and optimum-preservation properties require separate, problem-specific analysis. These operations can also appear within a decomposition. Their mathematical exactness and the implemented solver’s guarantees must be assessed separately.

sections.heading: Approximation guarantees and evidence for advantage.
sections.text: Approximation guarantees remain problem-specific. For maximum-cut on unweighted 3-regular graphs, one-layer ( p = 1 p=1 ) QAOA guarantees an expected approximation ratio (cut weight divided by the optimum) of about 0.6924 ( Farhi et al., 2014b ) ; classical semidefinite methods guarantee about 0.87856 on general graphs with nonnegative edge weights, including the unweighted case ( Goemans and Williamson, 1995 ) , and at least 0.9326 for unweighted graphs of maximum degree three ( Halperin et al., 2004 ) . E3LIN2 (Max-3XOR) maximizes satisfied three-variable parity equations; the early one-layer QAOA guarantee for its bounded-occurrence variant ( Farhi et al., 2014a ) stimulated a stronger classical guarantee ( Barak et al., 2015 ) . Numerical tests on random Max- k k XOR, its k k -variable generalization, find a classical mean-field method matching or outperforming QAOA on average in the tested regimes ( Müller et al., 2025 ) . Neither the preceding approximation guarantees nor these numerical observations establish implemented system advantages. More favorable evidence comes from several distinct regimes. For low-autocorrelation binary sequences, noiseless simulations found better empirical scaling than the tested exact classical solvers, together with small hardware demonstrations ( Shaydulin et al., 2024 ) . For random 8-SAT (Boolean satisfiability with eight literals per clause) near the satisfiability threshold, a fault-tolerant resource analysis combines QAOA with amplitude amplification, which increases the probability of measuring a satisfying assignment, and projects a runtime crossover under explicit assumptions on error correction and classical computational resources ( Omanakuttan et al., 2025 ) . For maximum-cut, classically warm-started, regularized QAOA has favorable hardware quality comparisons under matched algorithmic restrictions and a projected fault-tolerant crossover against stronger unrestricted classical heuristics ( He et al., 2026 ) . A further analysis gives better cut-fraction guarantees (fraction of edges crossing the partition) than the compared classical local algorithms for maximum k k -cut on specified regular graphs with girth (shortest cycle length) at least 2 ​ p + 2 2p+2 , where p p counts QAOA layers and vertices are partitioned into k k sets to maximize crossing edges ( Apte et al., 2026 ) . These studies contribute empirical scaling evidence, resource projections, and comparisons of provable guarantees; their assumptions and the distinction from demonstrated end-to-end advantage must remain explicit.

sections.heading: Fault-tolerant primitives and decoded quantum interferometry.
sections.text: Fault-tolerant primitives offer prospective guarantees: resource estimates for optimization heuristics ( Sanders et al., 2020 ) and near-quadratic branch-and-bound speedups under search-tree and oracle-access assumptions ( Montanaro, 2020 ) . Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) uses interference and an associated classical decoding problem to bias sampling toward good solutions. Its provable separation concerns folded optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), an approximate optimization problem over a finite field 𝔽 q \mathbb{F}_{q} with q q elements ( Kramer et al., 2026 ) . Polynomials of degree less than K K are represented by coefficient vectors c ∈ 𝔽 q K c\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{K} ; the evaluation points are grouped into M M blocks of size h h , and block i i has an evaluation matrix B i ∈ 𝔽 q h × K B_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{h\times K} and an acceptance set 𝒜 i ⊆ 𝔽 q h \mathcal{A}_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{h} . The problem is max c ∈ 𝔽 q K 1 M ∑ i = 1 M 𝟏 [ B i c ∈ 𝒜 i ] . \max_{c\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{K}}\ \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathbf{1}\bigl[B_{i}c\in\mathcal{A}_{i}\bigr]. Here 𝟏 ​ [ ⋅ ] \mathbf{1}[\cdot] is the zero–one indicator, and B i ​ c B_{i}c uses field arithmetic. The separation is not claimed for this general formulation. It holds for a growing family of folded Reed–Solomon instances whose block alphabets 𝔽 q h \mathbb{F}_{q}^{h} have superpolynomially many elements, with each acceptance set drawn independently and uniformly from the subsets containing exactly half of its block alphabet and accessible only through a membership oracle ( Kramer et al., 2026 ) . A membership oracle tests whether a block value belongs to 𝒜 i \mathcal{A}_{i} ; a coherent quantum query applies this test to a superposition without measuring the queried value. For a family with code rate K / ( M ​ h ) → R = 0.3 K/(Mh)\to R=0.3 , DQI makes one coherent quantum query to each block oracle and its expected score converges to ( 1 + R ⁡ ( 2 − R ) ) / 2 ≈ 0.857 (1+\sqrt{R(2-R)})/2\approx 0.857 . Classical algorithms reach the threshold ( 1 + R ) / 2 = 0.65 (1+R)/2=0.65 with linearly many classical membership queries, but exceeding it by any fixed amount with constant probability requires superpolynomially many ( Kramer et al., 2026 ) . Separate classical Markov-chain Monte Carlo tests attain DQI target scores on sparse maximum-XORSAT and ordinary, unfolded OPI, with exponential empirical scaling for the latter ( Gil-Fuster et al., 2026 ) . These experiments do not test the folded-OPI oracle family above; that separation also does not concern QUBO instances. For the analyzed DQI construction on unweighted maximum-cut, any graph family supporting a constant asymptotic improvement over the random cut fraction 1 / 2 1/2 has enough structure for exact classical polynomial-time solution ( Parekh, 2026 ) . This limits that proposed advantage on maximum-cut, a QUBO special case, without proving a limitation for every QUBO or every DQI variant. Recent DQI screening criteria compare decoding assumptions with explicit classical baselines; candidate problems and finite-budget comparisons do not establish a general speedup ( Mazumder and Niroula, 2026 ) . Classical-output approximation guarantees must also account for parameter selection, preparation, measurement, decoding, and repetition ( Hadfield, 2026 ) ; oracle-query results alone do not establish an implemented hybrid solver’s wall-clock benefit.

sections.heading: 3.5 Hardware and physics-inspired platforms
sections.text: Quantum annealers from D-Wave implement the transverse-field evolution on superconducting qubits connected by a fixed sparse coupling graph. A problem whose graph does not match is minor-embedded: each logical variable becomes a chain of physical qubits, which consumes qubits and couplers ( Boothby et al., 2020 ) . For example, the Chimera graph couples each qubit to at most six others, while Pegasus permits degree fifteen ( Boothby et al., 2020 ) . Neutral-atom arrays hold individual atoms in optical traps and encode a binary choice in a ground state and a highly excited Rydberg state. Strong interactions suppress simultaneous excitation of nearby atoms, providing a native interface for MIS on unit-disk graphs, whose vertices are atom positions and whose edges join atoms closer than a specified distance ( Ebadi et al., 2022 ) . The excited atoms represent the selected vertices; finite interaction strengths and longer-range interactions affect how closely the physical evolution realizes this graph model. Other graphs require the penalty formulation of Section 3.2 or additional encodings. These devices return candidate configurations, whose objective and feasibility can be checked classically. Superconducting circuits also implement gate-based processors at IBM and Google ( Kim et al., 2023 ; Harrigan et al., 2021 ) , while IonQ and Quantinuum use trapped ions ( Wright et al., 2019 ; Moses et al., 2023 ) . Neutral-atom platforms likewise support both analog Hamiltonian evolution and digital gates ( Henriet et al., 2020 ) . Usable circuit width and depth depend on coherence, gate errors, connectivity, and compilation overhead ( Montanez-Barrera et al., 2025 ) . Optical platforms span quantum and classical regimes. Photonic quantum accelerators are being integrated into classical optimization pipelines ( Slysz et al., 2026b ; Slysz et al., 2026a ) . QCi’s Dirac-3 implements entropy computing with weak coherent light, photon counting, and electronic feedback; it optimizes discretized real variables and encodes combinatorial problems ( Nguyen et al., 2025 ) . Its reported optical components are classically simulable in principle. Other Ising solvers include optical coherent Ising machines ( McMahon et al., 2016 ; Honjo et al., 2021 ) , simulated bifurcation ( Goto et al., 2019 ) , and digital annealers ( Aramon et al., 2019 ) ; their common Ising objective does not imply common connectivity, precision, or cost. Large-scale comparisons make these machines relevant baselines ( Zeng et al., 2024 ) , but broad comparisons across applications and platforms remain incomplete. The Quantum Optimization Benchmarking Library ( QOBLIB ) addresses this gap with ten problem classes, shared instances, and classical reference results, allowing application-level comparisons across formulations and devices ( Koch et al., 2026 ) . Application-derived circuits can also guide hardware design: a fixed-parameter optimization benchmark measures how circuit width and depth affect the persistence of a signal distinguishable from random sampling, exposing coherence and execution-rate bottlenecks across processors ( Montanez-Barrera et al., 2025 ) . A complementary benchmark evaluates execution time and solution quality on optimization applications ( Lubinski et al., 2024 ) ; parameter-setting costs can be assessed through the stochastic-solver benchmarking framework ( Bernal Neira et al., 2025 ) discussed in Section 5 . Hardware performance under these workloads remains distinct from solver advantage against capable classical algorithms on the original problem. Table 1 summarizes the interfaces. Mathematical-programming baselines provide an established comparison for Ising processing units ( Coffrin et al., 2019 ) . Section 5 evaluates quality, resources, and attribution against the relevant classical alternatives. Solver family Problem class Guarantees Principal limitations Quantum annealing / analog quantum devices Unconstrained QUBO / Ising ( 3 ); native MIS on restricted geometric graphs Heuristic; adiabatic guarantee only in idealized limits Qubit count and connectivity; noise and finite temperature; embedding overhead Physics-inspired Ising machines Unconstrained QUBO / Ising Heuristic Restricted objective structure; coefficient precision; topology and coupling constraints; readout and control scaling; no broadly applicable guarantees Gate-based variational (QAOA) Unconstrained QUBO; some constraints via mixers Special-case ratios; early examples matched or exceeded classically Circuit depth and noise; classical parameter optimization is nonconvex Fault-tolerant primitives Broad, including search and branch and bound Conditional asymptotic speedups, e.g. near-quadratic branch and bound under search-tree and oracle-access assumptions Require fault-tolerant hardware not yet available at scale Table 1: Quantum and physics-inspired solver families. Near-term interfaces are narrow; fault-tolerant primitives are broader but require hardware not yet available at scale. Section 5 assesses component benefits and system comparisons separately.

sections.heading: 4 Hybrid quantum-classical decomposition
sections.text: Classical routine(s) coordination, verification, remaining structure Quantum / Ising routine sample low-energy states of a QUBO ( 3 ) dispatched piece (family-dependent): master, block, pricing, separation, sampling returned information (family-dependent): candidate assignments or family-specific oracle output Figure 5: Representative QUBO-based hybrid interface (Table 2 ). Native independent-set sampling and constraint-preserving circuits need not use an unconstrained QUBO interface. Classical checks turn candidates into feasible incumbents or valid witnesses. In quantum-master Benders, classical recourse supplies cuts and a verified master relaxation supplies the lower bound; Section 4.4 describes this allocation. Figure 5 separates the dispatched task from the returned information: a master assignment, pricing solution, block update, separation witness, or variational sample. The return arrow need not carry a bound or optimality certificate; classical coordination must establish the family-specific property needed to continue or stop. Tables 2 and 3 summarize these interfaces and guarantee conditions. Section 5 assesses their empirical value. Following Abbas et al. (2024) , we cover quantum subproblems within classical decomposition and classical preparation, training, and postprocessing of quantum routines.

sections.heading: 4.1 Sampling and variational orchestration
sections.text: QAOA orchestration tunes the 2 ​ p 2p circuit parameters through continuous nonconvex search, typically without a global certificate ( Farhi et al., 2014b ; Hadfield et al., 2019 ; Zhou et al., 2020 ; Hao et al., 2025 ) . The optimizer loop in Figure 4 illustrates this potentially costly classical search ( Nannicini, 2019 ) . For suitable graph families and shallow depth, tensor-network calculations can select QAOA parameters classically before quantum sampling ( Streif and Leib, 2020 ) ; training costs and the validity of transferring parameters between instances remain part of the assessment. The training objective can also emphasize good samples: conditional value at risk (CVaR) averages a chosen lowest-cost fraction of outcomes ( Barkoutsos et al., 2020 ) . The initial state, ansatz, and mixer (Section 3.4 ) determine which assignments the circuit can reach. A pairwise X ​ Y XY mixing step acts on two qubits: its evolution transfers amplitude between | 01 ⟩ |01\rangle and | 10 ⟩ |10\rangle , leaving | 00 ⟩ |00\rangle and | 11 ⟩ |11\rangle unchanged. Unlike a single-qubit X i X_{i} operation, this step preserves the number of ones and hence a fixed-cardinality constraint when starting from a feasible state ( Hadfield et al., 2019 ; Fuchs et al., 2022 ) . Feasibility does not imply that every feasible assignment is reachable at a chosen depth: bounds on reachable assignments apply to fixed feasible basis states and schedules of disjoint pairwise X ​ Y XY mixing within fixed-cardinality variable groups ( Ubale et al., 2026 ) . For MIS (Section 3.2 ), results establishing that suitable mixer controls can prepare an optimal state supply neither efficient parameter discovery nor an explicit circuit-depth bound ( Tsvelikhovskiy et al., 2026 ) . Portfolio benchmarks exercise variational orchestration on structured instances ( Brandhofer et al., 2023 ) , while quantum-enhanced greedy optimization combines sampling with repeated variable fixing ( Dupont et al., 2023 ) , connecting orchestration to the recursive reductions of Section 4.3 .

sections.heading: Sample-guided route construction.
sections.text: A preprint on fleet sizing with time windows constructs routes from sampled arc frequencies through classical path extraction and pruning on a directed acyclic graph ( Makansi and Bernal Neira, 2025 ) . Its minimum-fleet guarantee requires an exact initial solution of the full discretized fleet-sizing model, an arc-frequency threshold in ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) , and multiple-longest-path extraction; heuristic sampling alone does not supply this guarantee. This is orchestration of sampling and classical construction; it supplies routes rather than a pricing certificate.

sections.heading: 4.2 Graph and multilevel decomposition
sections.text: A QUBO is a weighted graph, making three approaches natural: multilevel coarsening, cut-set elimination, and exact divide-and-conquer. Subgraph methods solve small components on quantum computers and stitch the results together ( Shaydulin et al., 2019 ) ; multilevel methods coarsen, solve, and refine in analogy to classical multigrid ( Ushijima-Mwesigwa et al., 2021 ) , including a scheme for maximum-cut ( Angone et al., 2023 ) . The downward path in Figure 6 replaces the graph by fewer aggregate variables. Mapping a coarse assignment back supplies a candidate on the original graph; refinement seeks improvements under the original objective because aggregation need not preserve an optimum. original graph n n nodes coarsen fewer aggregate variables coarsest: solve QUBO on device refine candidate on original graph Figure 6: Multilevel QUBO coarsening: aggregate the graph, solve at the coarsest level, then interpolate and refine. Coarsening is approximate. Cut-set elimination ( Ponce et al., 2025 ) and recursive splitting ( Pelofske et al., 2021 ) have different preservation conditions; exactness requires the relevant component or leaf solves to be exact. Cut-set elimination ( Ponce et al., 2025 ) uses component value functions to construct a reduced, generally reweighted graph, exactly or approximately depending on the reduction and component solves. Both component and reduced-problem solves are interfaces whose accuracy matters. Approximation-loss bounds for classical sparsification and decomposition of nonnegative-weight maximum-cut target circuit resources and noise in trapped-ion compilations ( Moondra et al., 2026 ) . These guarantees control transformation error, not the quality of an arbitrary finite-depth QAOA output. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split maximum-clique and minimum-vertex-cover instances on vertices until the resulting QUBOs fit the connectivity and qubit limits of D-Wave quantum annealers ( Pelofske et al., 2019a ; Pelofske et al., 2019b ; Pelofske et al., 2021 ) . The early studies target the D-Wave 2X (1152 qubits; Chimera graph with 3360 couplers, each qubit coupled to at most six others) ( King et al., 2015 ) and the D-Wave 2000Q (up to 2048 qubits; Chimera graph with 6016 couplers) ( Pelofske et al., 2019a ; Boothby et al., 2020 ) . These are nominal architecture counts: fabrication defects leave some qubits and couplers inactive, for example 1097 qubits and 3045 couplers on one D-Wave 2X chip ( King et al., 2015 ) , and minor-embedding chains further reduce the usable problem size. The maximum-clique study therefore splits subgraphs until they have at most 46 vertices on the 2X and 65 on the 2000Q ( Pelofske et al., 2019a ) . Complete recombination with optimal leaf solves is exact, but annealing itself does not guarantee those solves. Classical branch-and-bound also provides the skeleton for hybrid knapsack and traveling-salesperson solvers ( Sanavio et al., 2024 ) and for a QUBO study ( Peng et al., 2025 ) . Their samplers propose incumbents; node closure requires certified optimality, infeasibility, or valid bound-based pruning, not sampling failure. Tree growth and coordination can remain the bottleneck ( Häner et al., 2024 ) . Software implementations of these interfaces are discussed in Section 4.6 . The SPLIT framework coordinates parallel subproblems through effective local-field updates (Section 3.1 ) and greedy sweeps, fixing outside-block variables when updating each block ( Vandelli et al., 2026 ) . Its experiments use IBM CPLEX , a classical mathematical-programming solver, to solve the subproblems and provide a baseline for decomposition; quantum subsolvers remain prospective, and the heuristic has no general convergence proof.

sections.heading: Quantum preprocessing.
sections.text: Short QAOA circuits can also prepare input for a classical solver rather than solve the problem directly. Quantum preconditioning transforms the input problem using correlations from a QAOA circuit, with circuit depth setting the level of preconditioning, and then passes the transformed instance to classical heuristics such as simulated annealing or the Burer–Monteiro method ( Dupont et al., 2025a ) . A constrained variant gives a mixed-integer programming solver an objective built from QAOA correlations while retaining the original hard constraint and evaluating incumbents under the original objective ( Ramesh et al., 2026 ) . Relax-and-round solvers can likewise replace a classical relaxation with QAOA correlations before classical rounding; with depth-one circuits this matches its classical counterpart on several problem families, and a modified rounding recovers the Goemans–Williamson performance on certain graphs ( Dupont and Sundar, 2024 ) . A self-consistent mean-field preprint instead splits an Ising problem into independent subproblems whose mutual influence is represented by an environment computed with a variational circuit ( Dupont et al., 2026 ) . Section 5 assesses the evidence, including circuit and transformation costs. A portfolio pipeline applies random-matrix preprocessing, modified spectral clustering, and risk rebalancing, using an approximate decomposition that also benefits classical solvers ( Acharya et al., 2025 ) . An MIS pipeline combines exact graph reduction by lazy clique removals with compatibility testing and embedding on Rydberg arrays ( Schuetz et al., 2025 ) . Symmetry reduction also applies to lattice problems. A lattice is the mathematical set { B ​ z : z ∈ ℤ n } \{Bz:z\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\} generated by the integer combinations of the linearly independent columns of a basis matrix B B . Its shortest vector problem is the integer quadratic program min z ∈ ℤ n ∖ { 0 } ⁡ ‖ B ​ z ‖ 2 2 = z ⊤ ​ B ⊤ ​ B ​ z . \min_{z\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\setminus\{0\}}\ \|Bz\|_{2}^{2}=z^{\top}B^{\top}Bz. Approximate shortest-vector problems on structured lattices motivate hardness assumptions in post-quantum cryptography. One method exploits the symmetries of those lattices to encode a reduced search space as a Hamiltonian and then applies VQE (Section 3.4 ) ( Schirman et al., 2026 ) . The algebraic reduction is exact within the selected subspace, while its qubit implementation also bounds the integer coefficients; neither restriction guarantees preservation of the global shortest vector. The reduction also applies to classical lattice algorithms. A multilevel QUBO study ( Maciejewski et al., 2024a ) uses extended Noise-Directed Adaptive Remapping, which relabels bits so device noise favors previously found good solutions, and relax-and-round subsolvers ( Dupont and Sundar, 2024 ) . A semidefinite-inspired pipeline likewise executes device-sized subcircuits within classical preprocessing and postprocessing ( Dupont et al., 2025b ) , with a companion circuit-execution study ( Maciejewski et al., 2024b ) . A quantum local-search method solves and merges small MIS neighborhoods ( Tomesh et al., 2022 ) . Shallow, fixed-parameter sampling can also steer classical search between energy basins ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) . A recent preprint rotates an active neighborhood frontier under classical control while keeping circuit width bounded ( Mendes de Araujo and de Abreu Faria, 2026 ) ; it is not treated as settled evidence.

sections.heading: Quantum relaxations and readout.
sections.text: Quantum random-access optimization (QRAO) encodes up to three binary variables per qubit, maximizes the energy of a generally non-diagonal Hamiltonian, and rounds measurements in several bases into assignments ( Fuller et al., 2024 ) . For unweighted maximum-cut, the Hamiltonian’s maximum energy bounds the optimal cut from above; a variational candidate energy need not. A randomized rounding guarantee assumes that the prepared state has energy at least as high as the optimal cut value; variational preparation need not satisfy this condition.

sections.heading: 4.3 Quantum-informed recursive reduction
sections.text: Recursive QAOA estimates spin correlations from repeated measurements: for spins s i , s j ∈ { − 1 , 1 } s_{i},s_{j}\in\{-1,1\} , the mean product ⟨ s i ​ s j ⟩ \langle s_{i}s_{j}\rangle indicates whether the sampled values tend to agree or disagree ( Bravyi et al., 2020 ) . A strong positive or negative correlation suggests fixing s i = s j s_{i}=s_{j} or s i = − s j s_{i}=-s_{j} ; substituting this relation eliminates a variable, after which QAOA is run again on the reduced instance. This repeated solve–reduce cycle is the recursion, and the suggested relation need not hold in an optimum. At QAOA depth p = 1 p=1 , meaning one cost-and-mixing round per quantum call, an iterative MIS construction produces the same operations and selections as classical greedy MIS ( Brady and Hadfield, 2024 ) . This is distinct from the number of recursive reductions; departing from that equivalence requires more QAOA rounds or modified selection rules. Quantum-informed recursive optimization generalizes this approach: measured single-spin means and pair correlations guide problem-specific classical reductions, with backtracking to repair earlier decisions ( Finžgar et al., 2024 ) . A constraint-aware shrinking and repair pipeline uses simulated variational routines without hardware and is discussed here as a mechanism example ( Sharma and Lau, 2025 ) . In qReduMIS, kernelization repeatedly applies classical graph reductions that preserve an optimum and record how to reconstruct it from the remaining graph, called the kernel ( Schuetz et al., 2026 ) . For example, an isolated vertex can be selected and deleted because it belongs to every maximum independent set. When no implemented exact reduction applies, sampled inclusion frequencies identify vertices to fix inside or outside the independent set; those heuristic decisions may enable further exact reductions, and the cycle repeats. This family combines recursive orchestration with exact and heuristic reductions. Kernelization preserves an optimum through known rules; a probability-guided fixing remains heuristic unless certified, exhaustively backtracked, or included in complete branch-and-reduce. The quantum routine supplies correlations or candidate fixings, while classical routines supply feasibility checks, kernelization, reconstruction, and sometimes backtracking. Section 5 examines the fixed-wrapper ablations that distinguish these contributions.

sections.heading: Block updates.
sections.text: ADMM splits variables into blocks coupled by consensus and alternates block and multiplier updates. Its convex theory ( Boyd et al., 2011 ) does not transfer automatically to mixed-binary variants. A mixed-binary ADMM architecture assigns a binary block to a quantum or Ising solver and continuous convex blocks to classical solvers ( Gambella and Simonetto, 2020 ) . Its variant-specific assumptions give stationary-point convergence for a soft-constrained augmented Lagrangian, without generally ensuring original feasibility or global optimality. The stated theorems assume exact QUBO solves; the paper discusses extensions with vanishing, summable errors, not arbitrary sampling errors. This architecture has also been applied to routing ( Harwood et al., 2021 ) . Variational methods that keep slack variables or Lagrange multipliers classical, introduced in Section 3.4 , apply the same division of labor inside a single algorithm ( Braine et al., 2021 ; Le and Kekatos, 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Master proposals and cut selection.
sections.text: In most cited Benders schemes, the quantum routine handles the binary master while a classical linear or convex subproblem generates cuts. Examples include mixed-integer programming ( Chang et al., 2020 ) , QUBO-encoded masters ( Zhao et al., 2022 ) , and centralized and distributed generalized Benders for unit commitment ( Gao et al., 2025 ) . For transmission-network expansion, embedding preprocessing, conservative handling of cut constraints, and stopping rules have been adapted to heuristic annealers ( López-Baños et al., 2026 ) . A neutral-atom master uses tightened continuous-variable bounds to limit qubit count, retaining classical linear recourse ( Naghmouchi and da Silva Coelho, 2024 ) . This architecture also targets transmission switching and verification of power-system neural networks ( Ellinas et al., 2024 ) . Other discrete-continuous methods place quantum-annealed combinatorial solves inside classical search ( Ajagekar et al., 2020 ) . Master-side cut selection in multi-cut Benders supplies a different QUBO interface ( Paterakis, 2023 ) , also explored with gate-based QAOA ( de Valk et al., 2026 ) . Keeping only valid cuts keeps the master a valid relaxation, but permanently excluding needed cuts can prevent convergence. Exact master and subproblem solves give the standard finite-convergence argument; safeguarded inexact variants can use other conditions ( Rahmaniani et al., 2017 ) . The quantum contribution in a master-sampling implementation is candidate generation: an encoded master assignment is decoded, checked against the current cuts, and passed to classical recourse. Valid dual solutions or infeasibility certificates generate the corresponding cuts, while a feasible original solution updates the incumbent. A sampled master objective is not a certified lower bound; termination requires a verified master bound or another valid stopping certificate, with a classical fallback when heuristic sampling fails to make progress. The quantum substitution therefore changes the master-search procedure, while cut validity and final certification retain their classical proof obligations.

sections.heading: Pricing and restricted masters.
sections.text: In column generation, neutral-atom sampling supplies pricing solutions for minimum vertex coloring while the restricted master remains classical ( da Silva Coelho et al., 2023 ) . For fleet assignment, engineered embeddings and pulses generate columns, followed by diversifying postprocessing ( Perron et al., 2026b ) . Emulated neutral-atom pricing also targets fidelity-constrained routing, with classical path validation and restricted integer-master recovery ( Naghmouchi et al., 2026 ) . A multi-agent pathfinding method reverses the roles: classical pricing generates paths and a quantum restricted master selects compatible sets ( Gerlach et al., 2025 ) . Its path-generation construction can accumulate a sufficient pool despite inexact master solutions; optimality of its branch-and-cut-and-price variant requires the specified restricted-master accuracy. In general, certified termination requires exact pricing or a reliable no-improving-column certificate. Failure of heuristic sampling to find an improving column is not such a certificate. A proposed exact vehicle-routing branch-price-and-cut framework encodes pricing and separation as QUBOs, using every returned solution below a cost threshold ( Wagner and Liers, 2026 ) . The experiments implement the master relaxation, pricing, and separation. Dantzig–Wolfe branch-and-price for refinery scheduling keeps the master and continuous subproblem classical, while binary pricing goes to an annealer through qbsolv ( Ossorio-Castillo and Pena-Brage, 2022 ) . Dual prices induce columns and branching restores integrality ( Barnhart et al., 1998 ) . Pricing optimality had to be verified afterward by a classical global solver, preventing premature termination from missed improving columns.

sections.heading: Cutting planes and augmentation.
sections.text: A cutting-plane preprint combines a linear programming (LP) bound and graph reduction for maximum weighted independent set with neutral-atom samples and sample-informed classical odd-cycle separation ( Perron et al., 2026a ) . For t t -perfect graphs, variable bounds 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 0\leq x\leq 1 , edge inequalities, and odd-cycle inequalities describe the independent-set polytope. Polynomial-time separation permits polynomial-time optimization with a suitable classical algorithm; it does not by itself bound the implemented cut-adding loop’s iterations. Another interface samples Graver-basis elements—integer kernel directions for improving a feasible solution while preserving its linear equalities—for augmentation in nonlinear integer programming ( Alghassi et al., 2019 ) . A global-optimality guarantee requires an objective class satisfying the relevant Graver optimality conditions (such as separable convex minimization) ( Alghassi et al., 2019 ) , a complete sufficient test set, and valid augmentation and stopping; sampling does not certify completeness.

sections.heading: Commercial interfaces.
sections.text: Hosted services execute models as well as build them. D-Wave Leap accepts binary and constrained quadratic models through hybrid solvers ( D-Wave Systems, 2022 ) , and nonlinear models through an interface with native constraints ( D-Wave Quantum, n.d.c ) ; the open-source dimod and Qiskit Optimization libraries of Section 3.2 instead construct and convert models for a chosen solver. Quantinuum Nexus instead exposes compilation, execution, and data management for user programs ( Quantinuum, n.d.b ) ; its Guppy documentation demonstrates a user-built QAOA loop for maximum-cut, with classical parameter optimization and a Selene emulator backend in the example ( Quantinuum, n.d.a ) . These interfaces place different responsibilities on the user: submitting a constrained mathematical model differs from constructing its quantum circuit and classical optimization loop. The patent record includes mixed-binary decomposition and discrete-continuous optimization ( Gambella et al., 2020 ; You and Ajagekar, 2023 ) , sample-guided variable fixing and decomposition into subproblems ( Karimi and Rosenberg, 2018 ) , and integration of quantum samples into classical branch-and-bound ( McGeoch and Bernoudy, 2024 ) . Vendor documentation and patents describe available interfaces or disclosed designs; they do not by themselves establish a quantum contribution to performance. Their dates and evidential status follow Appendix A .

sections.heading: 4.5 Reformulation into continuous cones
sections.text: Cutting-plane master (classical) relaxes the copositive dual; polyhedral outer approximation of the copositive cone Ising / QUBO oracle witness search: minimize z ⊤ ​ M ​ ( η ) ​ z z^{\top}M(\eta)\,z over encoded z ≥ 0 z\geq 0 candidate M ⁡ ( η ) M(\eta) sampled bits encoding candidate z z Figure 7: Copositive separation ( Brown et al., 2024 ) : classical verification converts a negative witness into a cut for the lifted formulation ( Burer, 2009 ) . The matrix M ⁡ ( η ) M(\eta) is determined by the dual master decision vector η \eta . The exact-oracle guarantee requires continuous separation; finite-grid encoding and heuristic sampling introduce distinct limitations (Section 4.5 ). Lifting moves a problem into a higher-dimensional formulation. Examples include Dantzig–Wolfe reformulation of linear programs ( Dantzig and Wolfe, 1960 ) , moment and sum-of-squares semidefinite hierarchies ( Lasserre, 2001 ; Parrilo, 2000 ) , and the exact completely positive representation of mixed-binary quadratic programs ( Burer, 2009 ) . A completely positive matrix has a factorization X = B ​ B ⊤ X=BB^{\top} with entrywise B ≥ 0 B\geq 0 ; a symmetric matrix M M is copositive when z ⊤ ​ M ​ z ≥ 0 z^{\top}Mz\geq 0 for every z ≥ 0 z\geq 0 . The completely positive reformulation relocates hardness into conic membership: non-copositivity testing is NP-complete ( Murty and Kabadi, 1987 ) , and strong membership of both the completely positive and copositive cones is NP-hard ( Dickinson and Gijben, 2014 ) . A copositive framework derives a dual with the same optimal value as the mixed-binary primal under stated assumptions; equality with the dual supremum does not imply dual attainment ( Brown et al., 2024 ) . In Figure 7 , the outgoing matrix M ⁡ ( η ) M(\eta) , determined by the dual master decision vector η \eta , defines the separation task; the return arrow carries a sampled encoding of a candidate vector z z . Classically decoding it and checking z ≥ 0 z\geq 0 and z ⊤ ​ M ​ ( η ) ​ z < 0 z^{\top}M(\eta)z<0 yields a valid separating cut for the continuous dual: one verified violation suffices. With an exact continuous separation oracle and appropriate bounded localization and tolerance assumptions, cutting-plane variants such as the ellipsoid method approximate the dual value with polynomial oracle complexity and classical overhead. The finite-bit implementation has a weaker interface: a negative grid witness still gives a valid cut, but even a certified zero grid minimum establishes only approximate nonnegativity when a discretization-error bound is available. Failure of heuristic sampling to find a violation provides no such certificate. The supplement derives a grid-error bound separately from the paper’s exact-oracle result; exact reformulation, discretization, and finite-solver accuracy remain distinct. Q-FW uses the same reformulation route with Frank–Wolfe: linear-minimization steps become QUBOs for an annealer ( Yurtsever et al., 2022 ) . Q-FW replaces a single static exact-penalty weight with a prescribed augmented-Lagrangian or quadratic-penalty schedule. Its stated convergence result assumes exact linear minimization, a nonempty feasible set, strong duality, and bounded dual iterates; heuristic annealer calls do not automatically satisfy these conditions, and finite-iteration rounding may require feasibility repair.

sections.heading: 4.6 Software for decomposition and reduction
sections.text: Software exposes which variables a decomposition releases, how it treats their coupling to the remainder, and how it reconstructs a complete assignment. Supplementary Table S7 catalogs 23 public implementations, distinguishing libraries, research prototypes, and educational code with inspected source versions and scope limits. This targeted inventory establishes implemented interfaces, not comparative performance or independently validated correctness. For block search, the archived qbsolv combines conditioned sub-QUBO updates with tabu search; its default subsolver is classical, with annealing optional ( Booth et al., 2017 ) . dwave-hybrid separates decomposers, samplers, and composers, supporting energy-impact, graph-traversal, and random neighborhoods ( D-Wave Quantum, n.d.a ) . QSplit orchestrates split–solve–aggregate workflows through StreamFlow ; current source offers graph, matrix, neighborhood, and macrovariable splitting, voting, and conditioned or consensus-based refinement ( Bifulco et al., 2027 ; QSplit contributors, 2026 ) . HADOF instead substitutes sampled marginal means for exterior variables, so its subproblems differ from exact restrictions at a fixed incumbent ( Sankar et al., 2025 ; Sankar et al., 2026 ) . The inspected DQAOA implementation proposes updates from principal submatrices and checks accepted bits against the full objective, without incorporating all omitted couplings into the local linear terms ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . Pasqal QUBO Solver builds device-layout subproblems, requires nonnegative off-diagonal coefficients, and solves remaining variables classically ( Pasqal, n.d. ) . The registered QUBODecomposition.jl package provides connected-component solves and bounded conditioned sweeps through Julia optimizer interfaces ( JuliaQUBO contributors, 2026 ) . Graph-specific implementations offer additional interfaces. ML-QLS and MLQAOA coarsen, solve, project, and refine graph problems; the latter also transfers QAOA parameters using graph representations ( Ushijima-Mwesigwa et al., 2021 ; Bach et al., 2024 ) . QAOA-in-QAOA merges maximum-cut subgraph assignments by optimizing whole-subgraph flips, while Neural QAOA squared learns partitioning and parameter initialization ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . These restricted merges are not arbitrary QUBO recombinations. For recursive reduction, OpenQAOA implements correlation elimination and reconstruction; the QIRO reference code and Qrisp provide problem-specific replacement rules, whereas the public qReduMIS solver targets atom-position MIS with Rydberg backends ( Sharma et al., 2022 ; Finžgar et al., 2024 ; Qrisp developers, 2026 ; Schuetz et al., 2026 ) . DASQA supplies clique and vertex-cover branching with configurable leaf solvers; exactness requires exact leaves and valid pruning ( Pelofske et al., 2021 ) . Preprocessing is another reusable layer: dwave-preprocessing exposes roof-duality persistencies and component solves, Qoolchain combines reductions with branching, and QUBOLite supplies implication-based fixings and reconstructable partial assignments ( D-Wave Quantum, n.d.b ; Orlandi et al., 2025 ; Mücke et al., 2025 ) . For constrained interfaces, Qiskit Optimization implements mixed-binary ADMM and recursive correlation reduction; HQC-Bend delegates Benders masters, whereas Logistiqs keeps master and recourse solves classical and delegates cut selection ( Qiskit Community, n.d. ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; de Valk et al., 2026 ) . These interfaces have different proof obligations. Even the word decomposition requires care: Quafu-Qcover decomposes QAOA expectation evaluation into local neighborhoods, rather than combining independently optimized blocks ( Xu et al., 2024 ) . Across implementations, exact child solves alone do not certify coupled problems; comparisons must evaluate reconstructed assignments under the original objective and count preprocessing, training, repair, and coordination costs.
