sections.heading: 5 Attributing performance gains
sections.text: A transformed pipeline can beat a monolithic quantum solver because of its classical wrapper, its quantum component, or their interaction. Three questions distinguish these explanations: • Component effect: does substituting a quantum routine improve performance within a fixed classical wrapper at a stated quality or resource budget? • System effect: does a separately optimized quantum-enabled pipeline outperform a separately optimized classical pipeline at comparable quality and resources, including all end-to-end costs? • Reduction–solver interaction: does a reduction have a more favorable effect on the quantum solver than on a classical comparator on a common performance and resource scale? A fixed wrapper may favor the solver for which it was designed; a system comparison permits each pipeline its own tuning. For an interaction, let Y ⁡ ( r , σ ) Y(r,\sigma) measure predeclared higher-is-better solution quality at a fixed common resource budget, where r ∈ { 0 , 1 } r\in\{0,1\} indicates absence or presence of a reduction and σ ∈ { Q , C } \sigma\in\{\mathrm{Q},\mathrm{C}\} selects the quantum or classical solver, respectively. Define the simple effects Δ Q = Y ⁡ ( 1 , Q ) − Y ⁡ ( 0 , Q ) \Delta_{\mathrm{Q}}=Y(1,\mathrm{Q})-Y(0,\mathrm{Q}) and Δ C = Y ⁡ ( 1 , C ) − Y ⁡ ( 0 , C ) \Delta_{\mathrm{C}}=Y(1,\mathrm{C})-Y(0,\mathrm{C}) , and their contrast Δ int = [ Y ⁡ ( 1 , Q ) − Y ⁡ ( 0 , Q ) ] − [ Y ⁡ ( 1 , C ) − Y ⁡ ( 0 , C ) ] . \Delta_{\mathrm{int}}=\bigl[Y(1,\mathrm{Q})-Y(0,\mathrm{Q})\bigr]-\bigl[Y(1,\mathrm{C})-Y(0,\mathrm{C})\bigr]. (5) A positive contrast means a more favorable reduction effect for the quantum solver relative to the classical comparator. An absolute quantum-solver improvement additionally requires Δ Q > 0 \Delta_{\mathrm{Q}}>0 ; report both simple effects alongside the contrast. Neither condition implies system superiority. This factorial contrast is not automatically causal: assignment, tuning, and resource comparability determine that interpretation. Uncertainty must cover the declared contrast itself. The alternative of cost at a fixed quality target, estimators, and bootstrap procedures appear in the supplementary methods. Stochastic solvers add a further requirement: their parameters must be set, and the cost of setting them counts toward the comparison. A benchmarking framework scores parameter-setting strategies through the statistics of a declared performance metric across resource budgets ( Bernal Neira et al., 2025 ) ; its open-source stochastic-benchmark package supports designing, evaluating, and visualizing such strategies ( Bernal Neira et al., 2026 ) . Effect type and evidence status are distinct. A component comparison may use hardware, simulation, or nominal sample counts; a system comparison may report complete, partial, or projected timing. Following established benchmarking cautions ( Rønnow et al., 2014 ) , this survey counts end-to-end cost as preprocessing, parameter setting, mapping, queueing, communication, execution, decoding, verification, repair, classical coordination, and postprocessing where applicable. A strong classical comparator is one identified within this survey’s search, including relevant graphics processing unit (GPU) and physics-inspired methods at comparable quality. Tables 4 and 5 retain each study’s design, comparator, metric, and timing boundary; Appendix A gives the survey scope and version policy.

sections.heading: Wrapper benefits and component effects.
sections.text: Controlled swaps distinguish useful quantum information from quantum superiority. Within the same graph reduction, exact classical and QAOA component solves produce similar observed mean approximation ratios, near 0.96 versus about 0.75 for monolithic QAOA ( Ponce et al., 2025 ) . These observations support a reduction benefit, not formal equivalence or general solver insensitivity. Both arms retain QAOA as the final solver, so neither is an entirely classical control. In qReduMIS, quantum-informed reduction beats random selection and the wrapper improves on standalone optimized quantum annealing, yet SaReduMIS matches or exceeds the quantum arm on all 39 tested union-jack instances (site-diluted square grids with nearest and diagonal-neighbor edges) ( Schuetz et al., 2026 ) . SaReduMIS’s observed success probability of one on this testbed is not a guarantee; 500 replicas and two simulated-annealing steps versus 1,000 quantum measurements are nominal counts, not matched time or energy. The gate-based portfolio extension also supports a wrapper benefit, but retains QAOA in its comparator: 100 standalone shots and 20 hybrid trials with repeated calls use different budgets. Cumulative-shot time-to-solution excludes classical and communication costs and does not uniformly favor the wrapper on hardware ( Yalovetzky et al., 2026 ) . Positive and negative component findings coexist. In a Frank–Wolfe graph decomposition, simulated QAOA improves sparsity or error in the tested settings; IBM hardware beats simulated annealing at 50 and 70 nodes but loses at 100, without end-to-end timing ( Pennington et al., 2025 ) . Partitioned QAOA extends this approach to 1,710 edge variables assembled from circuits of at most 50 qubits; with shared repair, it reports lower residual error than the tested annealing and random samplers, without repeat-based uncertainty or matched computational costs ( Liaqat et al., 2026 ) . By contrast, specialized classical subproblem methods run faster than the quantum alternatives in pricing and separation experiments ( Wagner and Liers, 2026 ) . These experiments implement the master relaxation and associated subproblems motivated by an exact branch-price-and-cut framework, not the complete integer solver. Simulated annealing is the strongest sampler in the emulated cutting-plane wrapper ( Perron et al., 2026a ) . In small power-grid decompositions, ideal variational sampling fails to improve on uniform sampling with the same continuous solver even when quantum evolution is charged zero time; this negative result is restricted to the 5–13-generator, convergence-selected set ( Gaidai and Mukherjee, 2026 ) . Classical coordination also determines whether the selected quantum task merits its cost. In five toy hybrid pipelines, QAOA cut selection simulated classically with matrix product states consumes 99.3% of wall time, although cut selection takes a small share of the classical baseline’s runtime; a separate IBM experiment demonstrates only the component ( de Valk et al., 2026 ) . In emulated neutral-atom pricing, classical initialization narrows backend differences, and combined initialization and refinement bring the quantum arm’s mean gaps below 1% of CPLEX optima. Neither wall-clock comparison nor exact final pricing is established ( Naghmouchi et al., 2026 ) . In surveillance routing, a fixed-tour-pool comparison finds no systematic benefit of emulated neutral-atom selection over classical selection controls; the headline comparison against a full routing MIP projects QPU time from emulation, without hardware execution or complete pipeline costs ( Lauwerier et al., 2026 ) . Varying quantum-call frequency without a matched zero-quantum arm and complete accounting ( Holliday et al., 2026 ) cannot isolate the marginal component contribution.

sections.heading: Preconditioning and co-design.
sections.text: For the preconditioners described in Section 4.2 , accounting boundaries determine how much improvement can be attributed to the full pipeline. On random 3-regular maximum-cut, the reported benefit includes correlation construction through emulation, while the hardware demonstration remains limited ( Dupont et al., 2025a ) . For constrained bipartitioning, near-optimal incumbent discovery improves on 12–40 variables using classically evaluated correlations, whose construction cost is excluded ( Ramesh et al., 2026 ) . Main comparisons select each balance-penalty weight retrospectively to minimize that instance’s time to the known near-optimal target; global and cross-validated choices retain benefits with smaller depth-one gains. Rescoring on the original objective is essential because the surrogate need not preserve its optimum. Positive one-in-three Boolean satisfiability (SAT) at clause-to-variable ratio m / n = 0.626 m/n=0.626 supplies favorable co-design evidence ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . The restricting-space reduction improves the quantum methods relative to classical controls also given reduction-related information. Fits through n = 70 n=70 favor the reported quantum scaling bases, but quantum cost is inverse success probability whereas classical cost counts conflicts and propagations. The reduction also changes the search manifold, qubit count, Hamiltonian, and ansatz. Thus this predominantly simulated evidence is neither a fixed-wrapper swap nor an instance of Equation ( 5 ) on common resources. A 13-qubit experiment reaches 22-variable instances, without establishing a hardware crossover under complete wall-clock accounting.

sections.heading: System performance and accounting boundaries.
sections.text: High solution quality, device-access time, and complete system speed answer different questions. One superconducting study attains high approximation ratios, yet its projected run times trail the strongest classical heuristics, with no fixed-wrapper attribution ( Dupont et al., 2025b ) . In another, experimental samples steer a fixed classical search and reach global minima 2.23 times more often than tuned simulated annealing on the 20 hardest of 4,000 nearest-neighbor Ising instances under a projected 0.4-megahertz normalization ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) . The approximately 2.34-fold time-to-solution gain is fully projected against single-core simulated annealing, without GPU or planar-specific controls. On trapped-ion hardware, classically warm-started QAOA with local search attains higher quality and probability of finding an optimal cut than implemented Goemans–Williamson ( Goemans and Williamson, 1995 ) and Halperin–Livnat–Zwick ( Halperin et al., 2004 ) algorithms on five 96-node graphs, with local-search postprocessing also applied to classical outputs ( He et al., 2026 ) . Its runtime crossover against optimized rank-two Burer–Monteiro–Zhang heuristics ( Burer et al., 2002 ) , with classical local search and iterative refinement enabled, remains a fault-tolerant resource projection ( He et al., 2026 ) . Proprietary hybrids impose further attribution limits. One large dense-instance comparison normalizes accuracy by the best observed objective, hides the quantum/classical division, and times quantum processing unit (QPU) access while excluding reading, queueing, and local communication ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . Its reported quality and speed ratios therefore establish neither a component effect nor a complete system comparison. Hybrid and simulated annealing reach the optima on the certified small instances within a 139-instance maximum-cut benchmark, whereas direct QPU execution does not; larger-instance quality favors simulated bifurcation and slower simulated annealing ( Vodeb et al., 2026 ) . Heterogeneous hardware and some literature-sourced timings preclude a common-environment efficiency ranking. An audit of a portfolio service finds matches to all 54 certified head-to-head optima, with mean QPU access of 0.034 seconds in a five-second nominal budget ( Lozano, 2026 ) . The revised preprint’s matched-time tabu control has mean absolute objective gap 0.00078 to the service’s objective over 36 instances and 108 seeded runs. The small observable device-access share leaves the service’s remaining work and causal contribution unresolved. Selected comparisons nevertheless give restricted positive or mixed system evidence. A run-time benefit is reported on specially constructed sparse instance classes ( Tasseff et al., 2024 ) . Across 20 higher-order binary instances, the best energies over hybrid trials and settings match independently reported ground states on 14. At the hybrid’s mean solver-side runtime, several central processing unit (CPU) comparators fall short of these hybrid-defined targets on average, whereas enhanced parallel tempering and a GPU solver match or surpass them; orchestration and deployment costs remain excluded ( Chandarana et al., 2026 ) . Contextual classical controls further narrow interpretations. GPU quantum-annealing-inspired samplers improve sampling-time comparisons with quantum hardware and complete-pipeline comparisons with classical solvers on related multi-objective benchmarks; the complete quantum-system comparison remains unresolved ( Tao et al., 2026 ) . The largest industrial scheduling results in one study come from a classical Digital Annealer with cloud integration excluded ( Safi et al., 2026 ) . A product-state control is a useful candidate baseline, but best-of-ten cuts, trained schedules, and coloring excluded from timing prevent a matched advantage claim or general conclusion about entanglement ( Bantysh et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Scaling and reassessment.
sections.text: Scaling conclusions depend on the benchmark family and the classical frontier. The claimed scaling advantage in time to reach a relative objective gap ε \varepsilon , for targets of at least one percent on tailored high-precision spin glasses ( Munoz-Bauza and Lidar, 2025 ) , is closed by GPU simulated bifurcation ( Pawłowski et al., 2026 ) ; accessible sizes remain insufficient for robust asymptotic inference. Likewise, the reported superlinear speedup over optimized simulated annealing on hard native unit-disk instances ( Ebadi et al., 2022 ) is qualified by a classical reassessment that solves structured quasiplanar instances with thousands of vertices in minutes and obtains competitive simulated annealing results ( Andrist et al., 2023 ) . On harder families constructed through density and treewidth, quantum runs are slower on the small instances compared exactly; classical scaling suggests roughly 1,000 atoms at kilohertz repetition as a necessary step toward advantage, not an observed crossover ( Cazals et al., 2026 ) . Optimal adiabatic schedules are found to depend principally on independent-set instance difficulty rather than size ( Perseguers, 2025 ) . For gate-based methods, a QAOA scaling claim derives from idealized noiseless analysis and simulation; separate small-scale hardware demonstrations do not establish hardware scaling ( Shaydulin et al., 2024 ) . These distinct forms of evidence require distinct resource interpretations. The oracle model offers a complementary accounting check. The polynomial classical cutting-plane loop ( Brown et al., 2024 ) does not remove the difficult separation requirement. Holding the outer algorithm fixed isolates the oracle contribution; changes in iteration count and classical overhead, as well as oracle cost, require separate accounting. Polynomial overhead can itself remain costly in dimension, tolerance, and conditioning. The analyzed corpus supports conditional component benefits, useful wrapper improvements, and favorable co-design evidence, alongside negative comparisons and classical reassessments. It does not establish robust, transferable system superiority under full end-to-end accounting against the strongest relevant comparable classical baselines considered. Here robustness concerns repeated instances, seeds, hardware runs, and settings with uncertainty; transfer concerns independently generated or held-out instances. Those conclusions are scoped to the purposive survey, and do not negate its component findings. Declaring the effect, quality target, and timing boundary makes future comparisons interpretable; QOBLIB provides classically hard problem classes and solution records for such comparisons ( Koch et al., 2026 ) . sections.heading: 6 Design lessons and outlook
sections.text: The surveyed methods suggest three concrete questions for constraint programming and operations research.

sections.heading: Certified progress.
sections.text: When should sampling yield to classical certification? Benders needs lower bounds, column generation needs final pricing, and copositive separation must distinguish a negative witness from certified absence. Schedule certification adaptively, comparing its cost with progress from additional samples. Logic-based Benders and inference duals offer a language for specifying the proofs required at these interfaces.

sections.heading: Constraint-aware reduction.
sections.text: Which reductions preserve feasibility or an optimum, and which need repair, backtracking, or certified implications? Constraint-preserving mixers, classical masters, Lagrangian interfaces, and projection methods offer alternatives to large static penalties; their comparison should include encoding cost, accessibility of useful feasible states, and the consequences of implementation error.

sections.heading: Cost-aware interface selection.
sections.text: Is the quantum task still a bottleneck after preprocessing, communication, verification, and repeated calls? Fixed-wrapper substitutions, independently tuned complete systems, and four-cell reduction comparisons answer complementary questions. Specify the returned object, target, comparator, and accounting boundary before interpreting a gain.

sections.heading: Community contributions.
sections.text: Constraint programming and operations research can contribute established empirical discipline. The DIMACS implementation challenges ( Johnson and Trick, 1996 ) , the international SAT solver competitions ( Järvisalo et al., 2012 ) , and the MiniZinc Challenge ( Stuckey et al., 2014 ) compare solvers on shared instances under declared resource limits. Curated libraries such as MIPLIB ( Gleixner et al., 2021 ) and QPLIB ( Furini et al., 2019 ) supply instances with documented reference solutions and bounds. QOBLIB ( Koch et al., 2026 ) extends this effort to quantum optimization. These communities can contribute certified benchmarks, competition-style evaluations with complete resource accounting, and exact, bounding, and inference methods that certify feasibility and bound the quality of sampled candidates. Beyond benchmarking, these communities can help design the quantum computation itself: qubit placement and routing, gate scheduling, variational parameter optimization, and allocation of sampling and classical computation budgets. Statistical modeling and uncertainty quantification can support device calibration and control, while application expertise can identify useful structure and realistic decision requirements ( Bernal Neira et al., 2025b ) .

sections.heading: Appendix A Survey method
sections.text: This purposive survey uses topic queries, citation follow-up, and primary records to select decomposition, certification, and attribution studies through October 12, 2026; publication status was checked on October 12, 2026. The supplementary audit appended to this preprint gives methods, access limits, and Tables S1–S7; the source download and ancillary files provide source and audit data. These cover 30 studies (25 main-table entries), four historical exclusions, 82 discovery decisions, and an inventory of 23 software implementations. The survey is neither exhaustive nor an experimental reproduction.

sections.heading: Electronic Supplementary Material for: Quantum-Classical Hybrid Methods for Optimization: Lessons from Classical Decomposition
sections.text: Supplement to the manuscript prepared for Constraints , CPAIOR 2024 Master Class special issue. Tables S1 and S2 audit the 25 main evidence-table studies. Table S3 preserves 4 historical exclusion records. Table S4 records empirical source versions and publication-status checks for all 30 study records, including 5 contextual records. Table S5 records 82 discovery decisions from the targeted literature extension. Table S6 identifies source versions and passages for all 30 studies, distinguishing retained inspections from selective new checks. A contextual-record section and the complete data dictionary follow the tables. The evidence-eligibility cutoff is now October 12, 2026. The original cutoff June 30, 2026 and audit snapshot July 27, 2026 remain historical provenance. Targeted discovery covers July 1, 2026–October 12, 2026. Publication-status checks were refreshed on October 12, 2026; this does not imply that every empirical source was reread. New empirical audits and selective primary-text rereads identify the claims and versions inspected. The purposive update does not claim exhaustive literature coverage. The source-location index in Table S6 records the passages behind the main comparisons, including targeted corrections checked on October 6, 2026; these do not extend the eligibility cutoff. Component effects, system effects, and reduction–solver interactions support different inferences. Each row retains its design, comparator, target quality, and timing limits. A wrapper benefit or a favorable interaction can coexist with a faster classical system. A negative or unresolved component comparison remains informative; the audit does not impose one blanket advantage checklist on every study. The CSV files supplementary_studies.csv , supplementary_exclusion_log.csv , supplementary/literature-search.csv , and supplementary/claim-locations.csv are the source of truth. The tables and dictionary are rendered deterministically after identifier, field-coverage, inference-label, and source-location checks. The source download includes the standalone LaTeX source ( supplementary.tex ) and these records as ancillary files; the ancillary README.txt explains compilation and packaged filenames, and SOURCE_MANIFEST.json records the original paths and source checksums. Historical artifact labels are retained unless an explicit correction is recorded; blank artifact identifiers mean that no identifier was captured. A status check does not certify the underlying empirical claims or archival availability. No archival DOI has been assigned to this manuscript package by this update.

sections.heading: S1.1 Search scope, update history, and evidence records
sections.text: This is a narrative, purposive survey: studies were selected for their bearing on decomposition and attribution, rather than through exhaustive screening. Conclusions apply to the studies analyzed. The search combined Google Scholar and arXiv queries with publisher browsing across APS, Springer, Nature Portfolio, ACM, IEEE, Elsevier, and Taylor & Francis. Query families included “hybrid quantum classical optimization”, “Benders quantum”, “column generation quantum annealing”, “QUBO decomposition”, “graph coarsening QUBO”, “copositive optimization quantum”, and “quantum annealing benchmark”. The accompanying study audit records search routes and inclusion reasons; the exclusion log records close studies omitted from the evidence synthesis. These records document a purposive selection, not an exhaustive systematic search. The original corpus used an eligibility cutoff of June 30, 2026 and an audit snapshot dated July 27, 2026. A targeted update searched work first released or substantively revised from July 1, 2026 through October 12, 2026, extending the current eligibility cutoff to the latter date. Date-filtered topic queries and primary arXiv and publisher records covered decomposition, constrained optimization, preprocessing, controlled sampler comparisons, classical reassessments, and theoretical optimization guarantees. The update screened new studies as well as journal versions of older preprints; its queries, candidate decisions, and primary URLs accompany the supplement. This remains a purposive synthesis, with selections based on methodological relevance and extractable evidence rather than exhaustive coverage. Publication status was checked on October 12, 2026. First release, inspected empirical version, and current publication status are distinct fields. The October 4 pass retrieved arXiv lists ending with the October 2 listing; later releases may not then have been exposed. The October 12 refresh used date-qualified web searches over the same topic families, primary arXiv listings through October 12, and primary publication records; it did not repeat a Google Scholar search. The incremental window is October 5–12, including papers submitted earlier but first announced in this interval. Submission and listing dates are retained separately, and an October journal issue does not by itself establish an October first release. The update therefore documents what was found by the stated searches, not a complete census through the cutoff. Earlier empirical records are retained unless a specific reread is recorded; refreshing metadata alone does not revalidate every result. The SaReduMIS comparison in Schuetz et al. (2026) , first included in arXiv version 2 , and the expanded tabu control in Lozano (2026) , from version 3, postdate the original June cutoff but lie inside the extended scope. The graph-decomposition experiments of Pennington et al. (2025) are read from version 2. Version-specific citations identify inspected evidence when a later version could not be read. Patents and vendor documents describe the commercial record and are not treated as empirical evidence. Selective October 6, 2026 claim checks were recorded independently of the publication-status refresh. For [E11], Wagner and Liers, arXiv version 2 , Section 3, distinguishes the proposed complete framework from the implemented master relaxation; Section 5 and Figures 5–10 report pricing and separation quality and timing. For [A7], the journal version of Lu et al. (2026) , Table 1 and Scalings of time complexities , gives the reported scaling bases and their distinct quantum and classical cost measures; Figure 5 and Experiment on superconducting quantum processors locate the 13-qubit, 22-variable demonstration. The CSV records these local rereads separately from the corpus eligibility and publication-status dates. A study enters the evidence tables when its comparative design bears directly on component, system, or interaction effects. Mechanism papers and contextual counterpoints may be discussed without a main-table row. Labels [E1]–[E18] and [A1]–[A7] link the main article’s controlled-comparison and reassessment tables to supplementary_studies.csv . Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 report the associated scale, resource accounting, baseline, uncertainty, artifact, and certificate fields; S3 reproduces all four historical exclusion records; S4 records source versions and publication-status checks for all 30 study records, including five contextual studies. S5 records the extension’s candidate decisions, including mechanism papers without evidence-table rows. The supplement and supplementary_data_dictionary.md define the fields. The publication-status check log provides the primary URLs and the resolution of each check. These files accompany the article; no archival deposit identifier is claimed before one exists. Targeted October 7–12 checks preceded the global refresh and clarified background, theoretical guarantees, benchmark targets, and comparator roles. The October 12 refresh then checked all 28 existing study records and four historical exclusions, plus 27 other preprints (two overlap the exclusions) and three additional published or correction-sensitive references. The record of each check states its outcome and access limits; no new version or correction was located among the 32 existing study/exclusion records. The bibliography now cites the published VQEC journal article and Peng conference paper; these metadata upgrades do not establish stronger algorithmic or empirical guarantees. Newly selected comparisons have separate full-text extractions, while the prior empirical inspections, exclusion decisions, and 50 October 4 discovery records remain historical provenance. The ancillary files include the incremental queries and decisions, status-check reports, and source-location history in Table S6.

sections.heading: S1.2 Comparison design and resource accounting
sections.text: The main article’s attribution definitions follow established benchmarking cautions ( Rønnow et al., 2014 ) . A strong classical comparator means a relevant method identified within this survey’s scope at comparable target quality, including competitive GPU or physics-inspired implementations where applicable. It is a search-relative designation, not a claim of exhaustive baseline coverage. End-to-end time includes preprocessing, reformulation, embedding or compilation, queueing, communication, device execution or search, decoding, verification, and postprocessing whenever applicable. Solver-side pipeline time, device execution time, projected time, and nominal operation or sample counts are distinguished from that complete wall clock. The main article defines component and system effects. A fixed-wrapper swap estimates a component effect but may disadvantage a method whose wrapper was tuned to its original solver; system comparisons allow each pipeline its own tuning. To quantify a reduction–solver interaction, let Y ⁡ ( r , σ ) Y(r,\sigma) be a predeclared higher-is-better solution-quality statistic at one fixed resource budget, with r ∈ { 0 , 1 } r\in\{0,1\} indicating absence or presence of a reduction and σ ∈ { Q , C } \sigma\in\{\mathrm{Q},\mathrm{C}\} selecting the quantum or classical solver, respectively. All four cells use the same budget and resource-accounting boundary; achieved quality is measured, not fixed. The simple effects are Δ Q = Y ⁡ ( 1 , Q ) − Y ⁡ ( 0 , Q ) \Delta_{\mathrm{Q}}=Y(1,\mathrm{Q})-Y(0,\mathrm{Q}) and Δ C = Y ⁡ ( 1 , C ) − Y ⁡ ( 0 , C ) \Delta_{\mathrm{C}}=Y(1,\mathrm{C})-Y(0,\mathrm{C}) ; the main article defines their contrast as Δ int = Δ Q − Δ C \Delta_{\mathrm{int}}=\Delta_{\mathrm{Q}}-\Delta_{\mathrm{C}} . A positive contrast means a more favorable relative effect for the quantum solver, while an absolute improvement additionally requires Δ Q > 0 \Delta_{\mathrm{Q}}>0 . For example, Δ Q = − 0.1 \Delta_{\mathrm{Q}}=-0.1 and Δ C = − 0.3 \Delta_{\mathrm{C}}=-0.3 give a positive contrast of 0.2 0.2 although both solvers worsen. Report both simple effects with the contrast. Alternatively, at a fixed quality target, let T ⁡ ( r , σ ) T(r,\sigma) measure lower-is-better cost in the same resource units and accounting boundary for all four cells; cost is measured, not fixed. Use Δ int cost = [ T ⁡ ( 0 , Q ) − T ⁡ ( 1 , Q ) ] − [ T ⁡ ( 0 , C ) − T ⁡ ( 1 , C ) ] . \Delta^{\mathrm{cost}}_{\mathrm{int}}=\bigl[T(0,\mathrm{Q})-T(1,\mathrm{Q})\bigr]-\bigl[T(0,\mathrm{C})-T(1,\mathrm{C})\bigr]. (S1) A positive cost contrast means a more favorable relative cost effect for the quantum solver. An absolute quantum cost reduction additionally requires T ⁡ ( 0 , Q ) − T ⁡ ( 1 , Q ) > 0 T(0,\mathrm{Q})-T(1,\mathrm{Q})>0 ; report both solvers’ cost reductions alongside the contrast. Neither contrast sign implies that the quantum-enabled system outperforms the classical system. These are factorial contrasts, not automatically causal estimates: assignment, tuning, and resource comparability determine that interpretation. The statistic may be an expectation over randomness, an instance average, a median, or a per-instance quantity, but these choices are not interchangeable for heavy-tailed distributions. With cell estimates μ ^ r , σ Y \widehat{\mu}^{Y}_{r,\sigma} of the quality statistic Y Y , estimate Δ ^ int = ( μ ^ 1 , Q Y − μ ^ 0 , Q Y ) − ( μ ^ 1 , C Y − μ ^ 0 , C Y ) . \widehat{\Delta}_{\mathrm{int}}=\bigl(\widehat{\mu}^{Y}_{1,\mathrm{Q}}-\widehat{\mu}^{Y}_{0,\mathrm{Q}}\bigr)-\bigl(\widehat{\mu}^{Y}_{1,\mathrm{C}}-\widehat{\mu}^{Y}_{0,\mathrm{C}}\bigr). (S2) For cell estimates μ ^ r , σ T \widehat{\mu}^{T}_{r,\sigma} of the cost statistic T T , reverse the differences: Δ ^ int cost = ( μ ^ 0 , Q T − μ ^ 1 , Q T ) − ( μ ^ 0 , C T − μ ^ 1 , C T ) . \widehat{\Delta}^{\mathrm{cost}}_{\mathrm{int}}=\bigl(\widehat{\mu}^{T}_{0,\mathrm{Q}}-\widehat{\mu}^{T}_{1,\mathrm{Q}}\bigr)-\bigl(\widehat{\mu}^{T}_{0,\mathrm{C}}-\widehat{\mu}^{T}_{1,\mathrm{C}}\bigr). Report uncertainty for the declared contrast itself over both instances and solver randomness. A paired bootstrap resamples four-cell instance records and recomputes the declared statistic and contrast; resampling precomputed instance contrasts suffices for a mean contrast, but not generally for a difference of medians. With stochastic runs nested in instances, a hierarchical bootstrap also resamples runs within each selected instance, preserving any pairing across cells. Mixed-effects models are another option. Time-to-target and gap-at-time profiles ( Lubinski et al., 2024 ) , together with stochastic-solver scoring ( Bernal Neira et al., 2025 ) , make the quality–cost trade explicit. A benefit is robust when it replicates across instances, random seeds, hardware runs, and solver settings with stated uncertainty; it is transferable when it persists across generators or independently generated or held-out instances. Practical scale concerns classical difficulty at the target quality, not variable count alone. These criteria qualify each effect separately.

sections.heading: Contextual records and reconciliation notes
sections.text: These 5 cited empirical counterpoints have no row in the main evidence tables. Their records remain in the CSV and Table S4; their bounded interpretations are given here. Theory and method citations without an empirical audit appear in Table S5 where discovered by the update.

sections.heading: He et al., 2026
sections.text: Source: arXiv v1 (2026-03-10); hardware-comparator characterization selectively rechecked on 2026-10-04 Design: Five 96-node 3-regular graphs: hardware RWS-QAOA versus implemented GW and HLZ. Without local search it beats GW and approaches HLZ in approximation ratio; with local-search postprocessing also applied to classical outputs it surpasses HLZ, especially in success probability. Unrestricted strengthened Burer-Monteiro crossover is projected. Scope: Five 96-node 3-regular Max-Cut graphs for the hardware comparison. Supported inference: Measured solution-quality comparison with implemented GW and HLZ; unrestricted-system timing advantage remains projected. Timing: Measured hardware quality comparison; future fault-tolerant runtime crossover against unrestricted strengthened Burer-Monteiro is a projection, not a measured current-hardware speedup. Certificate: Optimal reference cuts define comparison metrics; the quantum routine does not itself certify optimality.

sections.heading: Tao et al., 2026
sections.text: Source: arXiv:2604.26477v2 (May 20, 2026); selective timing-scope reread October 6, 2026 Design: contextual counterpoint: sampling-time comparison with reported quantum hardware results (Figure 1); complete-pipeline comparison with classical DCM and DPA-a (Figure 2); complete quantum-system comparison unresolved Scope: closely related multi-objective benchmarks (cited counterpoint) Supported inference: Classical sampling and pipeline counterpoint; complete quantum-system comparison unresolved. Timing: Figure 1 compares sampling time; Figure 2 includes Ising model construction, sampling and Pareto filtering for the classical quantum-inspired pipeline versus classical baselines; complete quantum-pipeline times are not established Certificate: Not applicable

sections.heading: Safi et al., 2026
sections.text: Source: arXiv:2607.13325v1 Design: Industrial scheduling assignment QUBOs with classical sequencing, varied formulations/platforms; small exact baseline, time-limited references and classical heuristics. No isolated quantum-component replacement. Scope: Industrial scheduling with alternative compact and constraint-rich assignment formulations. Supported inference: Limited platform/formulation comparison; quantum component attribution unresolved. Timing: Paper labels execution end-to-end but explicitly omits communication latency, API overhead, queueing. Shared scaling trend is not matched elapsed time. Certificate: Quantum assignment/sequence split heuristic; exact branch-and-bound reference only on tractable cases; larger references time-limited.

sections.heading: Bantysh et al., 2026
sections.text: Source: arXiv:2609.15738v1 Design: Classical product-state projection after two-qubit updates; approximate MPS analysis and GSet quality versus literature best-known cuts. Not a matched whole-system solver race. Scope: GSet Max-Cut and small random-graph entanglement studies. Supported inference: Constructive classical baseline in fixed-parameter expanding-depth regime; no general conclusion about quantum optimization or entanglement. Timing: Fixed-schedule timing covers projected evolution and excludes graph coloring. Quality is the best cut among 10 runs; reported time is the mean per run. Tuning times identify the first best hit during an approximately one-hour search. Certificate: Heuristic product-state solver; best-known reference cuts do not certify optimum.

sections.heading: Gaidai and Mukherjee, 2026
sections.text: Source: arXiv:2607.15543v1 Design: Ideal variational binary sampler versus Uniform and SMAC, sharing the continuous CasADi/IPOPT subproblem; separate monolithic SCIP comparison at 5 generators. Scope: Generated AC optimal-power-flow/unit-commitment instances. Supported inference: Negative component result on small ideal simulations: trained sampling gives no incumbent-quality benefit over uniform. Not a universal no-advantage claim. Timing: Equal charged budget per size with quantum simulation time removed entirely. This favorable zero-quantum-time assumption is not hardware wall-clock evidence. Certificate: Heuristic nonconvex inner optimization; no global original-problem certificate established by hybrid sampling.

sections.heading: Dates and scope
sections.text: Expanded evidence eligibility cutoff: October 12, 2026. Publication-status check date: October 12, 2026. Original cutoff: June 30, 2026. Historical audit snapshot: July 27, 2026. The targeted literature extension covers July 1, 2026 through October 12, 2026, with searches assessed in America/New_York. These dates govern different operations. Original-cutoff statuses and historical source versions are preserved; new inclusions and selectively reread claims record their inspected version. The update includes targeted discovery, publication checks, and empirical inspection of selected sources, not a claim of exhaustive coverage. Source-location verification dates are recorded per claim, distinguishing retained earlier inspections from later selective passage checks; they do not extend the eligibility cutoff or imply a new corpus-wide publication-status check.

sections.heading: Reconciliation and generation
sections.text: The 30 study records comprise 25 main evidence-table records and 5 contextual records with row_id "-". citation_key is unique even for contextual records. Tables S1 and S2 render the evidence-table audits; Table S4 renders all study version/status records. Table S3 renders 4 historical exclusions. Table S5 renders 82 current discovery decisions. Table S6 indexes the inspected source versions and passages for all 30 studies. The CSVs are the source of truth. Tables S1-S5 and this dictionary are rendered deterministically after checking identifiers, schema coverage, inference-label agreement with the main tables, and publication-status fields. Table S6 is rendered from supplementary/claim-locations.csv after checking complete study coverage. The source download supplies the standalone LaTeX source and ancillary CSV records; the ancillary README.txt explains compilation and packaged filenames, and SOURCE_MANIFEST.json records original paths and source checksums.

sections.heading: Supported effects
sections.text: A component effect compares solvers inside a fixed wrapper; a system effect compares complete pipelines at a stated resource boundary and target quality; a reduction-solver interaction asks whether the reduction changes relative performance. Wrapper benefit and negative or unresolved comparisons are informative findings. Each claim is assessed at its own scope; a single blanket component-resolved end-to-end standard is not applied to every study.

sections.heading: Label conventions
sections.text: "Not reported by the authors" asserts an absence only when the source was inspected for that field. "Not applicable" marks a field without meaning for that comparison. "Not found by this survey’s documented search" and "not found by this survey’s search of the study text" describe search limitations. "Not extracted from the study by this survey’s audit" describes an audit limitation. Empty artifact identifiers mean no identifier was captured. Historical artifact labels and source-version descriptions are retained unless a documented correction says otherwise; a current publication check does not reverify them.

sections.heading: Inclusion policy and provenance
sections.text: A study enters the evidence synthesis when its comparative design can inform a component, system, or interaction effect, regardless of publication status. Mechanism studies may be discussed without a table row. The exclusion log records the historical purposive selection decisions and their present disposition, not an exhaustive census. The original source package remains in the recovery archive. No archival DOI for this manuscript package has been assigned by this update; a future deposit must be cited only after it exists.

sections.heading: Columns of supplementary_studies.csv
sections.text: row_id : Evidence-table identifier E followed by a positive integer or A followed by a positive integer. A hyphen marks contextual empirical records without a main-table row; citation_key remains unique. citation_key : BibTeX key in references.bib; the unique record key, including for contextual rows. authors_year : Short author-year label for the inspected empirical source. A publication-status change does not silently replace that source version. venue : Venue attached to the empirical audit; current_venue separately records a later verified bibliographic venue. version_inspected : Empirical source version underlying the current retained claims. A publication-status refresh alone does not replace this version; an explicitly documented selective reread may do so. Unpinned historical labels remain identified as such. prior_version_inspected : Exact version_inspected text preserved from the recovered July 2026 CSV. Empty for studies newly added by the October literature extension. status_at_original_cutoff : Historical publication status at the original June 30, 2026 eligibility cutoff, preserved when the current cutoff expands. Newer studies record that they were not yet public then. Retrospective acceptance dates alone do not establish public availability. status_at_prior_verification : Status recorded in the historical July 27 audit snapshot, formerly status_at_submission. New additions are marked as absent from that historical audit rather than reconstructing a check that was not performed. identifier : DOI or arXiv identifier recorded with the historical audit/citation. For post-cutoff journal citations the empirical version is still distinguished in version_inspected. search_route : How the study entered this purposive survey, including historical review routes or the targeted literature extension. The latter discovery decisions are recorded in supplementary/literature-search.csv. inclusion_reason : Reason the study informs the decomposition lens or a component, system, or reduction-solver interaction effect. quantum_role : Task assigned to the quantum routine, or an explicit absence of a quantum routine in classical reassessments. classical_role : Tasks assigned to classical routines and controls. comparison_design : What the study holds fixed and varies. Whole-system comparisons do not become component comparisons merely because a pipeline is described. instance_family : Problem family, sizes, and counts retained in the audit. target_quality_definition : Objective-quality or success target used in the comparison; its definition is needed before comparing resource use. timing_boundary : Included and excluded resources. Standard terms are full end-to-end wall clock, solver-side pipeline time, device execution time, projected time, and nominal operation or sample count. No timing claim is distinct from any timed comparison. uncertainty_reporting : Variability or uncertainty reporting captured by the audit. An audit limitation is not evidence that the study lacks uncertainty analysis. hardware_software_versions : Hardware, solver, software-version, and parameter information at the resolution actually captured by the audit. certificate_status : Independently checkable witnesses or certificates, their provider, and limits. The main evidence tables do not contain a certificate column; this field supplies that detail. artifact_status : Controlled vocabulary: archival dataset; source-code repository; input-data repository; available on request; publisher supplement; not reported; not found by documented search. This identifies the reported artifact class, not an independent audit of its contents; artifact_note retains scope and access limits. artifact_identifier : Known DOI or repository reference. Empty means no identifier was captured; never substitute an invented archival DOI or a promise of a future record. supported_inference : Bounded interpretation aligned with the main evidence tables: wrapper benefit, component comparison, system comparison, interaction evidence, or unresolved attribution, with direction and qualifications where supported. These effects are assessed separately. scale_and_repetitions : Scale and repetition details supporting the audited comparison, recovered from the original supplement or inspected for a newly included study. baseline_hardware_and_stopping_rule : Baseline implementation and stopping-rule details captured by the empirical audit; uncaptured details remain explicitly unspecified. artifact_note : Descriptive availability statement or explicit reconciliation note. artifact_status and artifact_identifier govern the displayed availability classification. audit_snapshot_date : Date of the audit snapshot when this record was created, not a claim that every empirical source was independently reread on that exact date. status_current : Publication status supported by the current check, or an explicit unresolved/not-reverified description. It may differ from the empirical source version. status_check_date : ISO date of the current publication-status check or attempted check. A date alone does not mean verification succeeded. status_check_result : Controlled result: verified_primary_record; limited_primary_record; unresolved. The result concerns publication metadata, not an independent verification of all empirical claims. status_sources : Primary-record URLs supporting the check, separated by " | ". Inaccessible or inconclusive sources are identified in status_notes, not treated as successful verification. status_notes : Evidence, limitations, version availability, or explanation of the current status. No-journal-version-found is search-limited, not proof that no such version exists. current_identifier : Identifier of the publication record checked in the current refresh, when supported. Historical identifier and empirical version fields are retained separately. current_venue : Venue of the publication record checked in the current refresh, when supported. latest_version_at_status_check : Latest source version observed during the metadata check, when captured. Availability of a newer version does not make it the empirical source inspected. empirical_refresh_date : ISO date of an explicitly documented primary-text inspection for a new empirical inclusion or a selective reread; empty for metadata-only refreshes. empirical_refresh_note : Claims inspected, source URLs, corrections or new findings, and limitations. Scope is local to the stated claims, not a comprehensive empirical re-audit. reconciliation_notes : Corrections of drift between the historical CSV, supplement, and revised main article. The recovered original package remains available as provenance.

sections.heading: Columns of supplementary_exclusion_log.csv
sections.text: study : Authors and short title of the close but omitted study. identifier : Persistent identifier retained in the exclusion log. first_version_date : Historical first-version date used for eligibility; retain the recorded precision instead of inventing an exact day. why_considered : Recorded reason the study was close to the survey scope. why_excluded : Historical reason for omission from the evidence tables. This describes the purposive selection decision; absence of hardware, matched timing, or a component-isolating control is not a universal bar to inclusion of system or interaction evidence. exclusion_id : Stable historical exclusion-log identifier X followed by a positive integer, independent of evidence-table identifiers. citation_key : Main-bibliography key when the excluded study is cited there; empty when no corresponding citation is used. status_current : Publication status supported by the current check, or an explicit unresolved statement. status_check_date : ISO date of the publication-status check or attempted check. status_check_result : verified_primary_record, limited_primary_record, or unresolved; metadata scope only. status_sources : Supporting primary-record URLs separated by " | ". status_notes : Evidence and limitations of the check, without treating unavailable material as verified. review_disposition : Whether the historical exclusion was retained or changed in this revision, and the scope of that decision.

sections.heading: Columns of supplementary/literature-search.csv
sections.text: candidate_id : Unique stable identifier for a candidate considered in the targeted literature extension. citation_key : Main-bibliography key for included evidence or context; may be blank for screened-only or out-of-scope candidates. title : Title of the candidate source used in the discovery decision. source_url : Primary record or full-text URL supporting candidate identity and the stated decision. first_public_date : First public date verified for the candidate, ISO YYYY-MM-DD; blank if not verified. Submission and announcement dates can differ and are explained in reason when material. version_inspected : Exact source version inspected, with any access limit stated explicitly. A current record alone does not imply full-text inspection. version_date : Date of the inspected version, ISO YYYY-MM-DD; blank if not verified. discovery_route : Query family, citation-chaining route, existing-record refresh, or other documented route by which the candidate was considered. decision : Controlled vocabulary: include_evidence; include_context; screen_only; exclude_scope. This is a purposive editorial decision, not a verdict on correctness. placement : Main evidence row, manuscript discussion, or screen-only location; blank when no placement applies. reason : Relevance, supported inference, limitations, and reason for the decision. Distinguish source findings from audit judgments and date ambiguity. source_check_date : ISO date of the discovery check, not a claim of universal literature completeness or a full proof/empirical verification.

sections.heading: Columns of supplementary/claim-locations.csv
sections.text: row_id : Evidence-table identifier E1-E18 or A1-A7, matching supplementary_studies.csv. A hyphen marks a contextual record; citation_key remains unique. citation_key : Unique BibTeX/study key linking this source-location record to supplementary_studies.csv and the main manuscript. claim : Bounded numerical claim or comparison to locate, including its relevant comparator, resource boundary or scope qualification. source_version : Exact version used for the stated passage check. An author preprint used for detailed locators is distinguished from the cited journal record; this field does not silently replace the historical audit version. source_url : HTTPS primary-source URL for the inspected record or text. Multiple sources, when needed, are separated by " | ". locator : Specific abstract passage, section, table, figure, appendix or stable source anchor supporting the claim in source_version. verification_date : ISO date of the supporting inspection or retained documented check. This claim-level date is distinct from the corpus eligibility cutoff, publication-status date and the date the index was assembled. verification_basis : selective_primary_passage_check identifies a targeted primary-text inspection on verification_date; retained_prior_inspection identifies an earlier documented inspection carried forward without a new reread. new_study_inspection identifies a full-text extraction for a newly included study. None of these labels implies experimental reproduction. limitations : Access restrictions, version differences, retained-audit boundaries, resource-accounting qualifications and other limits on what the cited passage establishes.

sections.heading: S2 Software implementations of decomposition and reduction
sections.text: Table S7 records 23 public implementations inspected on October 9, 2026. This purposive software inventory is separate from the empirical audit and does not extend its eligibility cutoff. Inclusion requires a concrete implementation of subproblem optimization, reconstructable reduction, multilevel optimization, structural preprocessing, or a constrained outer/inner interface. Packages, research prototypes, and an educational implementation are identified separately; multiple algorithms within one package are not counted as separate tools. Source and documentation were inspected, but no package was installed, executed, independently validated, or benchmarked for this inventory. The short commit links identify inspected implementation files, not necessarily released versions; full hashes, additional source paths, and evidence notes are in supplementary/software-catalog.json . QUBODecomposition.jl version 0.1.0 was separately verified as registered and released on October 12, 2026; this does not change the implementation-inspection dates. The accompanying supplementary/software-screening.json records selected leads outside the table; no verified public source in this search does not imply that none exists. For example, Quafu-Qcover decomposes QAOA expectation evaluation into local neighborhoods; this is distinct from optimizing independent sub-QUBOs and merging their assignments ( Xu et al., 2024 ) . License labels transcribe the inspected project declarations rather than assess legal compatibility; a missing project license is reported as unidentified. Table S7: Public software implementing decomposition and reduction. Source inspection establishes scope, not comparative performance or certified software correctness. Software and artifact type Implemented mechanism Scope and guarantee limits Inspected source / declared license qbsolv Archived solver Alternates bounded, incumbent-conditioned sub-QUBO optimization with tabu search. The default subsolver is classical; an annealer can be substituted. ( Booth et al., 2017 ) Heuristic for coupled problems; exact subsolves alone do not certify the original optimum. Archived dependencies may require reconstruction. 7b71f11 Apache-2.0 dwave-hybrid Python framework Composable decomposers, samplers and composers implement energy-impact, graph-traversal and random neighborhoods, conditioned subproblems, and parallel solver portfolios. ( D-Wave Quantum, n.d.a ) A workflow framework, not a global certificate. Kerberos and LatticeLNLS workflows for geometrically structured interaction graphs are templates within this package, not independent software entries. ec17a70 Apache-2.0 QSplit Workflow framework Matrix, interaction-neighborhood, graph-partition and macrovariable splitting feed distributed solves and voting, with optional conditioned, mean-field or soft-consensus refinement. ( Bifulco et al., 2027 ; QSplit contributors, 2026 ) Aggregation and compression are heuristic. Matrix-tile dimensions need not equal logical variable counts; reconstruction must be evaluated on the original QUBO. 279aff6 MIT Pasqal QUBO Solver Python solver package DecomposeQuboSolver builds device-layout-compatible subproblems and delegates remaining variables to a classical solver. ( Pasqal, n.d. ) The inspected decomposition rejects negative off-diagonal coefficients. Layout-compatible local solutions do not supply a general global certificate. 5211de1 Pasqal MIT-derived agreement (research-limited patent grant) QUBODecomposition.jl Julia package Solves fitting connected components and otherwise performs bounded conditioned neighborhood sweeps through optimizer interfaces, with full-model objective checks and budgets. ( JuliaQUBO contributors, 2026 ) Component-wise exactness requires exact child solves; coupled sweeps remain heuristic. The manuscript author contributes to this package. c760d09 MPL-2.0 HADOF Public research prototype Iteratively forms sub-QUBOs using sampled marginal means for external variables, updates those means with sampling subsolvers, and combines final block samples. Sequential and parallel implementations support annealing and variational/circuit backends. ( Sankar et al., 2025 ; Sankar et al., 2026 ) Mean-field boundary substitution and final sample aggregation are heuristic; they do not certify the original QUBO optimum or preserve its full joint distribution. ced7ee4 No project license identified DQAOA (ORNL research implementation) Public research prototype Solves overlapping then randomly selected principal sub-QUBOs with QAOA, distributes subsolves with MPI, and incorporates proposed bits only when the full QUBO objective improves; a single-core variant is also provided. ( Kim et al., 2026 ) Principal submatrices omit fixed-exterior linear contributions; global objective checks safeguard accepted bits, but neither heuristic proposals nor MPI parallelism establish optimality or quantum advantage. 9ed1842 No project license identified QAOA-in-QAOA (QAOA squared) Public research implementation Partitions a weighted MaxCut graph, solves each small subgraph, then constructs a coarser graph whose binary variables choose whether to flip entire subgraph assignments. Repeats this contraction until the remaining graph fits the subsolver. ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) Merging exploits MaxCut complement symmetry and optimizes over retained subgraph assignments; it is not unrestricted exact QUBO decomposition. Paper approximation guarantees require their stated assumptions. 7704cfd Apache-2.0 Neural QAOA squared Research code and model weights Extends QAOA-in-QAOA with a learned, capacity-constrained graph partition and joint QAOA parameter initialization, followed by subgraph solution and hierarchical orientation merging. Includes classical partition policies, training code, evaluation drivers, and pretrained weights. ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) A learned heuristic: training, inference, and subsolver costs belong in comparisons. Its evaluated instance results do not establish general superiority or quantum advantage. fcbc0ab MIT CUDA-Q academic divide-and-conquer QAOA Executable educational example Recursively partitions MaxCut graphs, solves subgraphs with CUDA-Q QAOA, and solves a merger Hamiltonian that chooses whole-subgraph color flips; MPI distributes initial subgraph workloads across workers. ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) Teaching implementation with heuristic subsolves and aggregation; it is not a generic packaged QUBO decomposer, nor does distribution certify solution quality. 847ec2d Apache-2.0 AND CC-BY-NC-4.0 (source header) ML-QLS (ml_qls) research implementation Coarsens graph-partitioning and community-detection instances, solves a coarse model, projects the solution, and refines bounded local Ising subproblems through classical, annealing, or QAOA interfaces. ( Ushijima-Mwesigwa et al., 2021 ) Multilevel heuristic; local solves do not certify the original optimum. Historical dependencies require environment reconstruction. bc37627 No project license identified MLQAOA Research code and notebooks Coarsens Max-Cut graphs, solves the coarse problem, projects assignments, and refines small subproblems; graph representations select transferred QAOA parameters from stored reference instances. ( Bach et al., 2024 ) Heuristic Max-Cut workflow; spectral similarity and approximate local solves provide no global certificate. Code uses legacy simulator calls. 41ba8b8 No project license identified OpenQAOA Released Python SDK RQAOA ranks one- and two-spin expectation values, fixes spins or pair relations, rewrites the Ising problem, solves a small residual classically, and reconstructs complete solutions. Custom schedules and adaptive multi-elimination are implemented. ( Sharma et al., 2022 ; Bravyi et al., 2020 ) Correlation fixing is heuristic; exact solution of the residual does not certify the original optimum. Sampling accuracy and reduction choices matter. c6e7dd7 MIT QIRO reference implementation Public research prototype Quantum correlations guide problem-specific MIS and MAX-2-SAT simplification. The MIS implementation solves small disconnected components by enumeration; the MAX-2-SAT implementation offers backtracking. A separate RQAOA implementation handles quadratic Hamiltonians. ( Finžgar et al., 2024 ) Correlation-based choices can remove an optimum. Feasibility-preserving rules and local enumeration do not provide a global optimality certificate; optional backtracking is bounded heuristic search. 8fc8e95 No project license identified Qrisp QIRO Python framework module QIROProblem alternates QAOA sampling with user-supplied replacement routines and rebuilds cost operators, mixers and initialization. Supplied routines cover MIS, clique and MaxSAT; set packing is transformed to an MIS graph. ( Qrisp developers, 2026 ; Finžgar et al., 2024 ) Heuristic, problem-specific reductions require separate validation. The inspected workflow keeps the original register length, so logical simplification does not itself establish reduced hardware width. 30a266c EPL-2.0; conditional secondary GPL license qReduMIS Python research package Alternates exposed-clique MIS reductions with decisions inferred from sampled independent sets. Inset/outset strategies select likely included/excluded vertices, maintain an incumbent, and restart classical reduction on the remaining graph. ( Schuetz et al., 2026 ) Sample-guided fixing is heuristic despite exact classical rules. The inspected solver accepts atom-position MIS instances and implements Rydberg backends, not generic QUBO or weighted MIS. 43feb75 Apache-2.0 DASQA (DBK/DBR) research implementation Branches maximum-clique and minimum-vertex-cover graphs, applies problem-specific reductions and bounds, and delegates size-limited leaves to a user-supplied solver before reconstructing a solution. ( Pelofske et al., 2019a ; Pelofske et al., 2019b ; Pelofske et al., 2021 ) Exactness is conditional on exact leaf solves and valid pruning; substituting a heuristic annealer does not supply an optimality certificate. 78f0109 No project license identified dwave-preprocessing Python/C++ utility package Roof duality computes a lower bound and persistent assignments; fixing composites reduce and restore variables, while a component composite dispatches disconnected BQM components to child samplers. ( D-Wave Quantum, n.d.b ) Strong persistencies hold in every optimum; weak choices preserve at least one. Global component optimality still requires exact child solves. 5e653e1 Apache-2.0 Qoolchain Python/C++ research toolchain Combines persistency, probing and implication-graph reductions with strongly connected components and Shannon branching; exposes residual models, variable maps, persistent assignments and a lower bound. ( Orlandi et al., 2025 ) Inspected C++ interface accepts integer coefficients. Shannon branching can grow exponentially; preprocessing and a lower bound alone do not solve all residuals. 537490c MIT QUBOLite Python utility package Implements QPRO+ implication/persistency rules and partial assignments that apply fixings to an upper-triangular QUBO, retain an objective offset, and expand residual solutions. ( Mücke et al., 2025 ) Reduction utility, not a hardware decomposition engine. Residual optimization remains necessary; coefficient-compression utilities are a separate transformation. cbe57e0 No project license identified Qiskit Optimization Python optimization library ADMMOptimizer alternates binary QUBO and continuous solves. RecursiveMinimumEigenOptimizer separately eliminates correlation-selected variable relations and reconstructs solutions. ( Qiskit Community, n.d. ; Gambella and Simonetto, 2020 ) ADMM rejects binary-continuous objective coupling and requires compatible subsolvers; convergence is conditional. Correlation elimination is heuristic, not certified persistency. 65ce191 Apache-2.0 HQC-Bend (HQCMCBD) Python research solver Separates a binary master from continuous linear subproblems, generates one or multiple Benders cuts, and offers Gurobi, D-Wave CQM/BQM, OpenJij, and simulated-bifurcation master backends. ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) Heuristic master samples and finite encodings do not themselves certify MILP optimality; Gurobi and hardware access are external dependencies. 43e9d29 MIT Logistiqs (hqc-mcms-benders) paper reproduction package Keeps Benders master and dual subproblems classical while selecting candidate cuts through minimum-set-cover or maximum-coverage models solved by classical or QAOA backends. ( de Valk et al., 2026 ) Cut selection is a heuristic acceleration interface; MILP certificates depend on classical bounds and valid cuts. Some archived hardware data require paid services to regenerate. c4fb789 No project license identified
