Bernal Neira † † thanks: Davidson School of Chemical Engineering, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA. Email: dbernaln@purdue.edu . This paper develops and extends a tutorial delivered at the CPAIOR 2024 Master Class “Quantum Computing for CP, AI, and OR, and vice-versa” ( Bernal Neira, 2024 ) and is prepared for the associated special issue of Constraints . Abstract Quantum and physics-inspired solvers provide specialized sampling interfaces for Ising and quadratic unconstrained binary optimization models, but constrained optimization requires broader coordination and certification. This survey uses classical decomposition to analyze how such solvers can be integrated into hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. We distinguish formal decomposition, reformulation and reduction, and computational orchestration. For each interface, we ask what the transformation preserves, which assumptions make the outer method converge, and which certificates the implemented inner routine supplies. The central questions are whether that information meets the classical algorithm’s requirements and whether hybridization improves solution quality or total cost enough to justify its coordination overhead. Benders decomposition, column generation, graph reduction, and copositive methods illustrate this distinction by separating heuristic proposals from classical certification. We also distinguish component effects within a fixed wrapper, reduction–solver interactions, and comparisons between complete quantum-enabled and classical systems. The analyzed studies provide conditional component benefits and favorable co-design evidence, but do not establish transferable end-to-end superiority over strong classical comparators. The resulting framework identifies opportunities for constraint programming and operations research in structure-preserving design, safeguarded hybrid algorithms, and controlled benchmarking. Keywords: quantum optimization; hybrid quantum-classical algorithms; decomposition; constraint programming; certification; benchmarking. 1 Introduction Classical optimization makes discrete problems tractable by exploiting structure, coordinating tasks that are easier for suitable solvers, and combining their results. Quantum optimization adds specialized solvers that encode an objective in a physical system or a sequence of controlled quantum operations, then return sampled candidate assignments. Section 3.3 introduces these quantum terms for readers without a quantum information science background. Using them for general constrained models requires additional encoding, classical coordination, or both. Decomposition connects specialized solvers to broader algorithms through interfaces such as pricing, recourse evaluation, and separation. The output required at an interface may be a useful candidate, a valid inequality, or a certified bound. We ask which outputs a quantum routine can supply, which classical checks remain necessary, and whether the resulting hybrid improves quality or total computational cost, including coordination overhead, over suitable classical alternatives. Existing reviews describe Ising machines ( Mohseni et al., 2022 ) , the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) and its variants ( Blekos et al., 2024 ) , the wider opportunities and obstacles in quantum optimization ( Abbas et al., 2024 ) , and, in a recent preprint, learned control of adaptive quantum workflows ( Lau, 2026 ) . Our contribution is to analyze these topics jointly through interface requirements, guarantees, and performance attribution . Tables 2 and 3 apply this analysis to the surveyed algorithm families, distinguishing returned candidates from the certificates required for guarantees. Section 5 then assesses the reported studies through component comparisons, reduction–solver interactions, and complete-system comparisons. The resulting conclusions concern the purposive corpus described in Appendix A , with eligibility through October 12, 2026. Section 2 introduces the classical foundations; Section 3 maps mixed-integer models to Ising and QUBO form and introduces the quantum algorithms and hardware that accept them. Section 4 develops the hybrid architectures, Section 5 evaluates their evidence, and Section 6 identifies design questions for constraint programming and operations research. 2 Discrete nonlinear optimization and the classical success story 2.1 What can be expressed, and why it is hard Mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) is a very expressive modeling language. A general MINLP has the form minimize x , y \displaystyle\underset{x,y}{\operatorname{minimize}} f ⁡ ( x , y ) \displaystyle f(x,y) (1) subject ​ to \displaystyle\operatorname{subject\ to} g ⁡ ( x , y ) ≤ 0 , \displaystyle g(x,y)\leq 0, x ∈ ℝ n c , y ∈ ℤ n i , \displaystyle x\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{c}},\quad y\in\mathbb{Z}^{n_{i}}, with f f and g g possibly nonlinear and nonconvex. The n c n_{c} continuous variables represent quantities, the n i n_{i} integer variables represent choices, and nonlinear terms may represent physical relationships. Applications include process design, scheduling, and engineering optimization ( Biegler and Grossmann, 2004 ) . The convex-MINLP solver review ( Kronqvist et al., 2019 ) and the fifty-year perspective on MINLP and disjunctive programming ( Kronqvist et al., 2026 ) trace the algorithms and formulations behind this modeling capability. Even linear integer programming is NP-hard; practical methods exploit instance structure, whereas quantum Ising/quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) interfaces require additional encodings to represent the constrained form above. This survey focuses on a single objective. Quantum multiobjective methods can instead explore trade-offs by approximately solving or sampling scalarized problems with different objective weights ( Kotil et al., 2025 ) . Many interface and certification considerations below apply to those subproblems, although solving individual scalarizations does not by itself certify a complete Pareto front. 2.2 Decomposition as the engine of progress Master problem complicating (integer) variables y y Subproblem remaining variables x x , with y y held fixed trial values y ^ \hat{y} optimality / feasibility cuts Figure 1: Classical Benders coordination: the master proposes complicating variables y y ; classical recourse in x x returns valid cuts. Hybrid interfaces are compared in Section 4 . Classical solver studies report large aggregate gains from algorithms and hardware ( Bixby, 2012 ; Koch et al., 2022 ) ; they do not isolate decomposition’s causal share. Decomposition is one important way to exploit problem structure. The idea: split a problem into smaller or more tractable parts, then coordinate them. In Benders decomposition, fixing complicating variables leaves a linear subproblem whose dual generates cuts for a master problem ( Benders, 1962 ) . Generalized Benders extends this construction to nonlinear subproblems through convex duality, making it relevant to MINLP ( Geoffrion, 1972 ) . Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition reformulates a structured linear program over the extreme points and, when necessary, extreme rays of its blocks, pricing columns as needed ( Dantzig and Wolfe, 1960 ) ; this underlies column generation and branch-and-price ( Barnhart et al., 1998 ; Lübbecke and Desrosiers, 2005 ) . For convex MINLP under standard subproblem and regularity assumptions, outer approximation alternates between a mixed-integer linear master and continuous nonlinear subproblems, accumulating valid supporting linearizations until the bounds meet ( Duran and Grossmann, 1986 ) . For nonconvex MINLP, local linearizations need not give valid global bounds; deterministic global methods combine valid relaxations with domain partitioning and bound tightening to certify a solution ( Burer and Letchford, 2012 ) . In Figure 1 , the outgoing assignment fixes the complicating variables y y ; the return cuts exclude infeasible master choices or bound their recourse cost. These cuts improve the master’s relaxation, whereas a candidate assignment alone supplies no such bound. Other decompositions use different master variables and oracle interfaces, as summarized in Section 4 . Logic-based Benders provides a bridge to constraint programming: cuts follow from an inference dual, allowing subproblems whose proofs need not come from linear programming duality ( Hooker and Ottosson, 2003 ) . Surveys and textbooks develop the theory and implementation of these methods ( Rahmaniani et al., 2017 ; Conejo et al., 2006 ; Constante-Flores and Conejo, 2025 ; Conforti et al., 2014 ) . Their interfaces require more than candidate assignments: cut validity, bounds, and termination each have proof obligations. We adapt a classical decomposition taxonomy ( Constante-Flores and Conejo, 2025 ) into three composable structural descriptions: • Formal decomposition splits variables, constraints, or the search domain. Its duality-based forms include Benders ( Benders, 1962 ) , Dantzig–Wolfe ( Dantzig and Wolfe, 1960 ) , and augmented Lagrangian methods such as the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) ( Boyd et al., 2011 ) ; its recursive forms include branching with bound-based pruning, as in branch and bound ( Land and Doig, 1960 ) . • Reformulation and reduction transform the problem through penalty mappings, conic lifts, coarsening, or elimination. An exact reformulation preserves the relevant solutions and objective; an approximation may change them. A relaxation supplies a lower bound in minimization (upper in maximization) by enlarging the feasible region or underestimating (overestimating) the objective. • Orchestration coordinates routines through samples, parameters, or candidate solutions. For example, an outer optimizer can tune the parameters of a quantum routine using the objective values estimated from its outputs; this parameter-tuning loop can itself be nested inside a decomposition. Section 4 uses these categories to distinguish formal master–subproblem methods, graph and conic reformulations, and sampling or parameter-tuning orchestration. They identify algorithmic structure, not mutually exclusive guarantee classes. An exact conic reformulation can support cutting-plane methods ( Brown et al., 2024 ) or Frank–Wolfe updates ( Frank and Wolfe, 1956 ; Yurtsever et al., 2022 ) , but heuristic inner solves require separate convergence justification. Conversely, a formal decomposition may lack its classical guarantee when convexity, oracle accuracy, or certified pruning assumptions fail. We therefore assess three questions independently: what the transformation preserves, which assumptions make the outer method converge, and which certificates the implemented inner routine supplies. The practical lesson is to assign each solver a task that exploits structure and whose output can be verified. Smaller subproblems can help, but duplicated work, many iterations, or lost global structure can erase that benefit. Dimension reduction alone establishes neither computational savings nor a potential quantum contribution. 3 Quantum and physics-inspired solvers for Ising and QUBO problems This section first states the classical models that Ising and quantum solvers accept and how mixed-integer problems can be translated into them (Sections 3.1 and 3.2 ). It then introduces the quantum concepts used in the rest of the article (Section 3.3 ), the main quantum optimization algorithms (Section 3.4 ), and the hardware and physics-inspired platforms that run them (Section 3.5 ). 3.1 The Ising and QUBO substrate Here the Ising objective is the energy of a finite, classical, pairwise spin model on a graph G = ( V , ℰ ) G=(V,\mathcal{E}) , with vertices V V and edges ℰ \mathcal{E} : E ⁡ ( s ) = ∑ i ∈ V h i ​ s i + ∑ { i , j } ∈ ℰ J i ​ j ​ s i ​ s j , s i ∈ { − 1 , 1 } . E(s)=\sum_{i\in V}h_{i}s_{i}+\sum_{\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{E}}J_{ij}s_{i}s_{j},\qquad s_{i}\in\{-1,1\}. (2) The real coefficients h i h_{i} are external fields, or single-spin biases, and J i ​ j J_{ij} are pairwise couplings; their signs are included in the coefficients. Fixing spins in a set V fix ⊆ V V_{\mathrm{fix}}\subseteq V leaves each remaining spin i i with the effective local field h i + ∑ j ∈ V fix : { i , j } ∈ ℰ J i ​ j s j h_{i}+\sum_{j\in V_{\mathrm{fix}}:\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{E}}J_{ij}s_{j} , its new linear coefficient. Under the displayed plus-sign convention, J i ​ j < 0 J_{ij}<0 favors aligned spins (a ferromagnetic coupling), whereas J i ​ j > 0 J_{ij}>0 favors opposite spins (an antiferromagnetic coupling). The graph and coefficients are problem data, with no restriction to a regular interaction graph or couplings of one sign. This specifies the optimization model within the broader physics tradition of Ising ferromagnets and disordered spin glasses ( Ising, 1925 ; Sherrington and Kirkpatrick, 1975 ) . Finding a ground-state configuration means minimizing E ⁡ ( s ) E(s) . The affine substitution s i = 2 ​ x i − 1 s_{i}=2x_{i}-1 , with inverse x i = ( s i + 1 ) / 2 x_{i}=(s_{i}+1)/2 , maps spin assignments bijectively to bits and converts the energy into an equivalent quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem min x ∈ { 0 , 1 } n x ⊤ ​ Q ​ x , \min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\quad x^{\top}Qx, (3) where n = | V | n=|V| and Q ∈ ℝ n × n Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is symmetric. Off-diagonal entries are half the coefficients of the equivalent upper-triangular convention because x ⊤ ​ Q ​ x x^{\top}Qx counts each pair twice. Linear terms occupy the diagonal, since x i 2 = x i x_{i}^{2}=x_{i} ; additive constants do not change the minimizer and are dropped. Conversely, substituting x i = ( s i + 1 ) / 2 x_{i}=(s_{i}+1)/2 into x ⊤ ​ Q ​ x x^{\top}Qx gives ( 2 ), up to a constant, with J i ​ j = Q i ​ j / 2 J_{ij}=Q_{ij}/2 for i < j i<j and h i = 1 2 ​ ∑ j Q i ​ j h_{i}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}Q_{ij} . The maximum-cut problem partitions vertices into two sets to maximize the weight of crossing edges. With nonnegative edge weights w i ​ j w_{ij} , it maximizes ∑ { i , j } ∈ ℰ w i ​ j ​ ( 1 − s i ​ s j ) / 2 \sum_{\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{E}}w_{ij}(1-s_{i}s_{j})/2 , since an edge contributes exactly when its spins differ ( Goemans and Williamson, 1995 ) . Negation gives, up to a constant, a zero-field Ising minimization with J i ​ j = w i ​ j / 2 J_{ij}=w_{ij}/2 ; the affine substitution above produces a QUBO. A physical solver returns samples from a device- and protocol-dependent distribution, typically without an optimality certificate. Ising-oriented devices include quantum annealers, optical and analog machines, and digital accelerators, with applications in optimization and engineering ( Mohseni et al., 2022 ; Bernal et al., 2022 ) ; Section 3.5 describes these platforms. 3.2 From mixed-integer programs to QUBO Constrained problem min ⁡ f ⁡ ( x ) \min\;f(x) s.t. A ​ x ≤ b Ax\leq b x ∈ { 0 , 1 } n x\in\{0,1\}^{n} Penalized form min ⁡ f ⁡ ( x ) \min\;f(x) + ρ ​ ∥ A ​ x + S ​ w − b ∥ 2 +\,\rho\,\lVert Ax+Sw-b\rVert^{2} slack bits w w , u = S ​ w u=Sw QUBO min ⁡ ( x , w ) ⊤ ​ Q ​ ( x , w ) \min\;(x,w)^{\top}Q\,(x,w) additional bits, coefficient range constraints into objective absorb slacks, tune ρ \rho Figure 2: Constraint-to-QUBO mapping for integer or scaled-rational data and a quadratic objective (after any required quadratization). Exact slack encoding u = S ​ w u=Sw , with binary slack bits w w and encoding matrix S S , requires bounded ranges commensurate with the encoding; arbitrary real coefficients need not admit it. Here Q Q acts on the concatenated bits ( x , w ) (x,w) . Slack bits are auxiliaries; squaring the penalty introduces pairwise couplings, and weights satisfying ( 4 ) preserve optima. The larger model and coefficient range can worsen conditioning and increase the selected solver’s resource requirements. The MINLP ( 1 ) is the natural starting point for these mappings: the task is to represent general integer, continuous, and nonlinear structure, not only to penalize constraints. Standard catalogs and modeling tutorials describe the resulting formulations ( Lucas, 2014 ; Glover et al., 2019 ) . Reaching ( 3 ) involves four steps, each with its own cost. Below, x x denotes the encoded binary vector. First, each integer variable is written in binary: for z ∈ { L , … , U } z\in\{L,\ldots,U\} , a binary encoding is z = L + ∑ k = 0 m − 1 2 k ​ b k z=L+\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}2^{k}b_{k} , with m = ⌈ log 2 ⁡ ( U − L + 1 ) ⌉ m=\lceil\log_{2}(U-L+1)\rceil and b k ∈ { 0 , 1 } b_{k}\in\{0,1\} . If the bit range exceeds U − L U-L , the constraint ∑ k 2 k ​ b k ≤ U − L \sum_{k}2^{k}b_{k}\leq U-L or a bounded encoding must exclude excess values. Second, continuous variables must either be discretized, which introduces an additional approximation, or remain with a classical solver; the latter is the decomposition route of Section 4 . Third, nonlinear terms must become quadratic. Once the variables are binary, every real-valued function of them has an exact multilinear polynomial representation, for example e b = 1 + ( e − 1 ) ​ b e^{b}=1+(e-1)\,b for b ∈ { 0 , 1 } b\in\{0,1\} , although the representation can need exponentially many terms; auxiliary variables that represent products, enforced by penalty terms, then reduce it to quadratic form ( Boros and Hammer, 2002 ) . Approximating a function to keep the model small is a separate modeling choice, distinct from the approximation introduced by discretizing continuous variables. Fourth, constraints can become objective penalties, but there is no universal encoding. A linear equality can use ρ ​ ( a ⊤ ​ x − b ) 2 \rho(a^{\top}x-b)^{2} ; an inequality can first introduce a nonnegative slack, whose exact positional binary encoding requires bounded, commensurate values, as in integer or scaled-rational data. Reading Figure 2 from left to right reveals two resource costs: slack bits enlarge the assignment, and squaring a constraint introduces pairwise couplings between its variables. A compact constrained model can therefore become a denser QUBO with a wider coefficient range. Direct penalties can avoid slack bits when the constraint has suitable structure: for binary variables, ρ ​ x i ​ x j \rho x_{i}x_{j} penalizes exactly the violation of x i + x j ≤ 1 x_{i}+x_{j}\leq 1 . One-hot encodings assign one bit to each allowed integer value and require exactly one selected bit; they use more bits than positional encodings but can simplify selection constraints. Higher-order violation penalties may instead require quadratization auxiliaries ( Lucas, 2014 ; Glover et al., 2019 ; Quintero et al., 2022 ) . Eliminating variables, preserving feasibility in the quantum algorithm (Section 3.4 ), or retaining constraints in a classical master (Section 4 ) offers alternatives to a single penalized QUBO. These choices trade variable count, coupling density, coefficient range, and proof requirements; large penalty weights stretch the range a physical solver must resolve, and samples can remain infeasible. Penalization changes the feasible domain, even when it preserves global optima ( Constante-Flores and Conejo, 2025 ) . Then, for 𝒳 ∖ F ≠ ∅ \mathcal{X}\setminus F\neq\varnothing , the penalized problem min x ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ f ⁡ ( x ) + ρ ​ P ​ ( x ) \min_{x\in\mathcal{X}}f(x)+\rho\,P(x) has the same global minimizers and optimal value as the constrained problem whenever ρ > max ⁡ { 0 , max x ∈ 𝒳 ∖ F ⁡ f ⋆ − f ⁡ ( x ) P ⁡ ( x ) } . \rho>\max\left\{0,\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}\setminus F}\frac{f^{\star}-f(x)}{P(x)}\right\}. (4) The threshold is finite but involves the unknown f ⋆ f^{\star} ; an arbitrary penalty weight need not preserve the optimum. If 𝒳 = F \mathcal{X}=F , any ρ ≥ 0 \rho\geq 0 suffices. One sufficient, possibly conservative bound is ρ > ( f ¯ − f ¯ ) / δ \rho>(\overline{f}-\underline{f})/\delta , where f ¯ ≤ f ⁡ ( x ) \underline{f}\leq f(x) on 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , f ¯ \overline{f} is the value of a known feasible solution, and every infeasible point has penalty at least δ > 0 \delta>0 . Problem-specific formulations can give sharper weights and smaller encodings; catalogs discuss many examples ( Lucas, 2014 ; Glover et al., 2019 ) , and the maximum k k -colorable subgraph analysis explicitly characterizes penalty choices and auxiliary-variable trade-offs ( Quintero et al., 2022 ) . The broader theory of Lagrangian reformulation distinguishes equality of optimal values from equality of minimizer sets and gives sufficient conditions for finite exact penalties ( Quintero et al., 2024 ) . In particular, a positive minimum penalty over infeasible points is automatic on the finite domain used in ( 4 ), whereas continuous domains can require limiting penalty sequences rather than a finite exact weight. Maximum independent set (MIS) illustrates the mapping. Given a graph G = ( V , ℰ ) G=(V,\mathcal{E}) , MIS asks for as many vertices as possible with no edge between two selected vertices; as a mixed-integer program (MIP), max ⁡ ∑ v ∈ V x ∈ { 0 , 1 } V ⁡ x v s.t. x u + x v ≤ 1 for all ​ { u , v } ∈ ℰ . \max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{V}}\ \sum_{v\in V}x_{v}\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad x_{u}+x_{v}\leq 1\quad\text{for all }\{u,v\}\in\mathcal{E}. Modeling software automates parts of this translation and differs in what it delivers. QUBO.jl supports mathematical-programming reformulations and solver access ( Xavier et al., 2026 ) ; Qiskit Optimization converts quadratic programs into QUBO form when they have no continuous variables, no quadratic constraints, and integer-valued coefficients in all linear constraints ( Qiskit Community, n.d. ) ; and D-Wave’s open-source dimod library represents binary and constrained quadratic models, converting a constrained model into a penalized binary model only when its constraints are linear and its integer variables have zero lower bounds ( D-Wave Quantum, n.d.a ) . PyQUBO supports symbolic QUBO construction and constraint-aware decoding ( Zaman et al., 2022 ) , and qubovert manages polynomial and constrained Boolean or spin formulations ( Iosue, n.d. ) . Fixstars Amplify SDK combines modeling and conversion with access to several quantum and classical solver backends ( Fixstars Amplify, n.d. ) . Such libraries build and transform models locally, whereas hosted solver services, discussed in Section 4.4 , also execute them. The interface automates parts of the translation; its choice alone establishes neither exactness of a penalty model nor a quantum contribution. 3.3 Quantum computation for optimization readers A classical bit takes value 0 or 1; a qubit is a quantum system with two distinguished states, written | 0 ⟩ |0\rangle and | 1 ⟩ |1\rangle . For n n qubits, the computational basis consists of 2 n 2^{n} mutually orthogonal vectors | x ⟩ |x\rangle , one for each binary assignment x x ; the ket notation | ⋅ ⟩ |\cdot\rangle denotes a state vector ( Nielsen and Chuang, 2010 ) . An ideal pure state is a normalized superposition | ψ ⟩ = ∑ x α x ​ | x ⟩ |\psi\rangle=\sum_{x}\alpha_{x}|x\rangle , where the complex amplitudes satisfy ∑ x | α x | 2 = 1 \sum_{x}|\alpha_{x}|^{2}=1 . Measuring in this basis returns one assignment x x with probability | α x | 2 |\alpha_{x}|^{2} , not all assignments at once. Repeated preparation and measurement produce samples. Unlike classical probabilities, amplitudes have phases: when combined, they can reinforce or cancel, producing interference that changes the sampling probabilities. A product state factors into individual-qubit states; a pure state that does not is entangled . A Hamiltonian H H is a Hermitian matrix (equal to its conjugate transpose) representing energy, with real eigenvalues. For a classical cost f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) , the diagonal problem Hamiltonian satisfies H C ​ | x ⟩ = f ⁡ ( x ) ​ | x ⟩ H_{C}|x\rangle=f(x)|x\rangle ; its lowest-energy, or ground, states encode minimizing assignments. Quantum evolution is the change of the amplitudes over time. For constant H H , ideal closed-system evolution applies U ⁡ ( t ) = e − i ​ t ​ H U(t)=e^{-\mathrm{i}tH} , where i 2 = − 1 \mathrm{i}^{2}=-1 , setting the reduced Planck constant ℏ = 1 \hbar=1 ; this linear map is unitary, meaning reversible and norm-preserving. Optimization algorithms choose these operations to make good assignments more likely upon measurement; doing so efficiently is the algorithmic challenge. Analog devices physically implement a Hamiltonian and vary its coefficients continuously. Figure 3 illustrates how energy levels change along such a path; Section 3.4 explains the annealing method. Gate-model computers compose quantum gates , unitary operations on one or a few qubits, into a circuit , followed here by measurement. A designed Hamiltonian evolution is implemented or approximated by such a gate sequence. The upper part of Figure 4 illustrates this circuit notation: each horizontal wire carries one qubit through operations ordered from left to right, and the final measurements produce the bits of one assignment. The gates marked 𝖧 \mathsf{H} prepare ( | 0 ⟩ + | 1 ⟩ ) / 2 (|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2} from each | 0 ⟩ |0\rangle ; these Hadamard gates are distinct from the Hamiltonian H H . Circuit width counts qubits; gate depth counts sequential layers of operations that cannot run in parallel. Gate platforms include superconducting circuits, trapped ions, photonics ( Bharti et al., 2022 ) , and neutral atoms ( Henriet et al., 2020 ) . Noise and control error perturb the ideal operations; fault-tolerant computation uses many physical qubits to encode logical qubits and correct errors, at substantial resource cost. Progress from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) regime, whose gates lack error-correction protection ( Preskill, 2018 ) toward early fault tolerance now includes demonstrations of error correction and logical operations, while large-scale fault-tolerant systems remain a development goal ( Bluvstein et al., 2026 ) . 3.4 Quantum optimization algorithms Adiabatic computation and quantum annealing. Adiabatic quantum computation starts from an easily prepared ground state and slowly changes the Hamiltonian, aiming to follow its evolving ground state ( Albash and Lidar, 2018 ) . Quantum annealing commonly uses H ⁡ ( t ) = A ⁡ ( t ) ​ H D + B ⁡ ( t ) ​ H C H(t)=A(t)H_{D}+B(t)H_{C} , decreasing the driver weight A ⁡ ( t ) A(t) while increasing the problem weight B ⁡ ( t ) B(t) ( Kadowaki and Nishimori, 1998 ) . The usual driver H D = − ∑ i X i H_{D}=-\sum_{i}X_{i} is a transverse field : X i X_{i} exchanges | 0 ⟩ |0\rangle and | 1 ⟩ |1\rangle on qubit i i , so this term couples assignments differing in one bit. Its ground state is the uniform superposition of assignments, also prepared by the Hadamard gates in the circuit example of Figure 4 . “Transverse” refers to its orientation perpendicular to the spin axis used for the diagonal Ising objective; its evolution redistributes amplitudes between assignments. In the circuit-based variational algorithms considered here, a classical optimizer adjusts parameters of a gate-based circuit. For each parameter choice, repeated executions estimate a training objective, often the expected problem cost ( Cerezo et al., 2021 ; Bharti et al., 2022 ) . An ansatz is the chosen family of states generated by the parameterized circuit; choosing it fixes the search space. The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) estimates the expected energy of a parameterized state and uses a classical optimizer to lower it, seeking the Hamiltonian’s smallest eigenvalue and an associated state ( Peruzzo et al., 2014 ) . For a cost Hamiltonian diagonal in the computational basis, this energy is estimated by the mean objective value of the sampled assignments. The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) typically starts from an equal-amplitude superposition of all assignments and applies p p layers, each a problem evolution followed by a mixing evolution ( Farhi et al., 2014b ; Zhou et al., 2020 ) . At layer ℓ \ell , the problem step e − i ​ γ ℓ ​ H C e^{-\mathrm{i}\gamma_{\ell}H_{C}} changes each assignment’s phase according to its cost; alone, it leaves sampling probabilities unchanged and is not a descent step. TikZ code prepared with OpenAI Codex assistance. Constraints inside quantum algorithms. Constraints that are not penalized can enter the quantum algorithm itself. The feasibility-preserving generalization of QAOA starts with amplitudes only on feasible assignments and uses mixers whose ideal transitions stay within that set ( Hadfield et al., 2019 ) ; implementation errors can violate this invariance. Linear Ising penalties use single-spin biases rather than extra pairwise couplings and can reduce connectivity and coefficient-range demands, with theoretical, simulation, and annealing-hardware evidence for the studied constraints ( Mirkarimi et al., 2024b ; Mirkarimi et al., 2024a ) . Embedding Lagrangian duality in adiabatic computation can avoid slack-variable encodings; in a fault-tolerant circuit implementation, the proposed construction has a qubit count independent of the number of constraints, while solution-sampling probabilities still depend on the duality gap and complementary slackness ( Gabbassov et al., 2025 ) . Variational methods can also keep multipliers or slack variables classical. A transaction-settlement method updates circuit parameters and nonnegative slack variables, with sample-informed slack adjustments intended to escape poor local solutions ( Braine et al., 2021 ) . A variational quantum eigensolver with constraints (VQEC) uses quantum estimates of costs, constraints, and gradients while a classical primal–dual method updates circuit parameters and Lagrange multipliers ( Le and Kekatos, 2024 ) . Its expectation-constrained formulations can admit distributions containing infeasible assignments, and its nonconvex parameter updates have no general global-convergence guarantee; individual samples still require the original feasibility checks. Quantum Zeno constraint enforcement instead repeatedly measures whether the state lies in the subspace spanned by feasible assignments, without identifying the full assignment. Frequent checks suppress transitions out of that subspace in the ideal limit; finite measurement rates and implementation errors must be assessed in practice ( Herman et al., 2023 ; Berwald et al., 2025 ) . Thus constraints can enter through objective penalties, dual multipliers, or restrictions on the quantum evolution. Linear penalty constructions need not satisfy the assumptions of ( 4 ); their feasibility and optimum-preservation properties require separate, problem-specific analysis. These operations can also appear within a decomposition. Their mathematical exactness and the implemented solver’s guarantees must be assessed separately. Approximation guarantees and evidence for advantage. Approximation guarantees remain problem-specific. For maximum-cut on unweighted 3-regular graphs, one-layer ( p = 1 p=1 ) QAOA guarantees an expected approximation ratio (cut weight divided by the optimum) of about 0.6924 ( Farhi et al., 2014b ) ; classical semidefinite methods guarantee about 0.87856 on general graphs with nonnegative edge weights, including the unweighted case ( Goemans and Williamson, 1995 ) , and at least 0.9326 for unweighted graphs of maximum degree three ( Halperin et al., 2004 ) . E3LIN2 (Max-3XOR) maximizes satisfied three-variable parity equations; the early one-layer QAOA guarantee for its bounded-occurrence variant ( Farhi et al., 2014a ) stimulated a stronger classical guarantee ( Barak et al., 2015 ) . Numerical tests on random Max- k k XOR, its k k -variable generalization, find a classical mean-field method matching or outperforming QAOA on average in the tested regimes ( Müller et al., 2025 ) . Neither the preceding approximation guarantees nor these numerical observations establish implemented system advantages. More favorable evidence comes from several distinct regimes. For low-autocorrelation binary sequences, noiseless simulations found better empirical scaling than the tested exact classical solvers, together with small hardware demonstrations ( Shaydulin et al., 2024 ) . For random 8-SAT (Boolean satisfiability with eight literals per clause) near the satisfiability threshold, a fault-tolerant resource analysis combines QAOA with amplitude amplification, which increases the probability of measuring a satisfying assignment, and projects a runtime crossover under explicit assumptions on error correction and classical computational resources ( Omanakuttan et al., 2025 ) . For maximum-cut, classically warm-started, regularized QAOA has favorable hardware quality comparisons under matched algorithmic restrictions and a projected fault-tolerant crossover against stronger unrestricted classical heuristics ( He et al., 2026 ) . A further analysis gives better cut-fraction guarantees (fraction of edges crossing the partition) than the compared classical local algorithms for maximum k k -cut on specified regular graphs with girth (shortest cycle length) at least 2 ​ p + 2 2p+2 , where p p counts QAOA layers and vertices are partitioned into k k sets to maximize crossing edges ( Apte et al., 2026 ) . These studies contribute empirical scaling evidence, resource projections, and comparisons of provable guarantees; their assumptions and the distinction from demonstrated end-to-end advantage must remain explicit. Fault-tolerant primitives and decoded quantum interferometry.
